units.title: The Four-Column Scheme of Work in Practice
units.summary: Use a four-column scheme of work with the columns Timeline and Objectives, Core Tasks and Skills, Resources and Technology, and Assessment Methods, and study a worked two-week example with eight lessons.

p: A scheme of work works best as a simple table with four columns. Each column answers one question.
• Column 1: Timeline and objectives. When will it happen, and what will students be able to do?
• Column 2: Core tasks and skills. What will students do, and which skills does it train?
• Column 3: Resources and technology. What do I need to teach it?
• Column 4: Assessment methods. How will I know students learned it, and what will I do with the information?

In Week 3 you used four columns for a whole module: theme and timeline, language focus, exam skill focus and assessment goal. This week we use a version made for daily teaching. Here is how they match:
• Theme and timeline becomes Column 1 (and you add objectives).
• Language focus and exam skill focus become Column 2 (core tasks and skills).
• New in this version: Column 3, resources and technology.
• Assessment goal becomes Column 4, with more detail about the method.

b: You can see the whole unit on one page.
You can check that every lesson has a task, a resource and a check.
Colleagues can read it and teach from it.

p: Write lesson numbers or dates, not only weeks. For example: Lessons 1 to 4 (Week 5). Then write one clear objective for each lesson or each pair of lessons.
Use 'I can' statements. Link them to syllabus skill codes.
Examples:
• Lesson 1 (R1, R3): I can find specific facts in a short article.
• Lesson 2 (W3): I can use five new adjectives in sentences.
• Lesson 3 (S2): I can speak for one minute on a topic with a reason.
• Lesson 4 (W2, W4): I can write an email that is organised and friendly.
If the objectives do not show a clear growth over the lessons, add steps. Lesson 4 should be harder than lesson 1.

b: Leave a small gap for review in each week.
Write the exam date and the mock date at the top.
Mark bank holidays and school events.

p: Core tasks are the main activities that train the skills. For each lesson, list two or three. Say which skill each one trains. Mark each as receptive (reading, listening) or productive (writing, speaking).
Example for one lesson:
• Task 1 (listening, receptive): listen to two short recordings and choose the best picture. Exercise 1 style.
• Task 2 (speaking, productive): in pairs, say which sport you prefer and why.
• Task 3 (writing, productive): write three sentences with 'because'.

Check across the whole unit: Is there a good balance of receptive and productive work? Do students practise all four skills each week? Is the Cambridge exam task type clear, for example Exercise 3 notes, or Part 2 short talk?
If a task is not obviously linked to a skill, ask why you are doing it.

b: Count receptive tasks and productive tasks across the unit.
If most are receptive, add a speaking or writing task.
If most are productive, add input first.

p: List everything you need for every task. This stops last-minute stress. Think about three kinds of resources.
• Texts and audio: past paper texts, textbook pages, a news article, a short recording.
• Materials you make: worksheets, picture cards, checklists, speaking cards.
• Tools and technology: a projector, a speaker, a phone voice recorder, a timer, a class shared folder.
Plan for places where technology is weak. For every digital resource, write a low-tech backup.
• If there is no projector, write the text on large paper or give each pair a printed copy.
• If there is no speaker for audio, read the script aloud yourself and record it on a phone first.
• If the internet is slow, download files before the lesson.
• If students have no phones, use pair talk and write notes on paper.
Keep a folder, on paper or on a computer, for each module. Put every resource in it with a clear name. The next teacher, or you next year, will thank you.

b: Do I have enough copies for the class?
Have I tested the audio?
Is there a backup if the technology fails?
Where is it saved?

p: Assessment tells you whether the lesson worked. Choose the method for each lesson.
Formative methods (during learning):
• Observation of pair work with a simple tally.
• Exit tickets: one question on a slip of paper.
• Quick quizzes of five questions.
• Peer checks with a checklist.
• Short writing marked with the Content and Language tables.
Summative methods (at the end of a unit):
• A past paper exercise marked with the mark scheme.
• A full mock paper.
• A recorded speaking test marked with the four criteria.
For each method write who marks (teacher, peer or self), what criteria are used, and what happens next (feedback, redo, reteach). Without the last part, assessment is just a score.

b: Quick check for understanding: exit ticket.
Practice of an exam skill: one exercise from a past paper.
Progress over time: a mock test every term.
Skill awareness for students: self-assessment checklist.

sections.h: A worked example: two weeks on 'Where we live'
p: Here is a full example for a class that meets four times a week. It is written for this course. The theme is housing and home life, which is common in the exam. The exam skills are Exercise 3 notes, Exercise 5 email and Paper 3 Part 2 talk.

Week 1, Lesson 1. Objective (R1, R3): I can find facts in a short article about homes. Tasks: skim and scan an article; answer six short questions; pair talk about your home. Resources: article, worksheet. Assessment: check answers together; exit ticket.

Week 1, Lesson 2. Objective (W3): I can use words for rooms, furniture and size. Tasks: word map; describe a picture; write five sentences. Resources: picture cards, vocabulary list. Assessment: peer check of sentences.

Week 1, Lesson 3. Objective (L2): I can understand opinions about living in a small home. Tasks: listen to three short speakers; match each speaker to an opinion; discuss. Resources: audio or script, speaker. Assessment: mini quiz.

Week 1, Lesson 4. Objective (S2): I can compare two options and say which I prefer. Tasks: look at a Part 2 style card (two types of home); one minute to prepare; speak for two minutes in pairs. Resources: card, timer. Assessment: peer feedback with two stars and a wish.
Week 2, Lesson 5. Objective (R1, R3): I can write brief notes under headings. Tasks: read a text about tiny homes; complete notes (Exercise 3 style). Assessment: mark with the key.
Week 2, Lesson 6. Objective (W2): I can link ideas with 'because', 'although' and 'however'. Tasks: link sentences; fix a paragraph. Assessment: exit ticket.

Week 2, Lesson 7. Objective (W1, W4): I can write an informal email that explains a problem with my home. Tasks: read a model; plan; write 120 to 160 words. Assessment: peer check, then teacher marks one draft.
Week 2, Lesson 8. Review. Tasks: improve the email using feedback; speak for one minute about a problem at home; five-question quiz on the unit. Assessment: quiz and reflection.

ex.t: What makes this a good unit
b: Every lesson has an objective, a task, a resource and a check.
The skills rotate: reading, writing, listening, speaking.
Each lesson prepares for the next.
The last lesson allows review and a second try.

units.title: Lesson Micro-Structure: Starter, Main Phases and Plenary
units.summary: Turn the syllabus into a 50 to 60 minute lesson with a starter, three main interactive phases and a plenary, using timings, a template and a full sample lesson on an informal email.

sections.h: What a 50 to 60 minute lesson looks like
p: A good lesson has a clear shape. Students know where they are, what they are doing and why. The shape has four parts: a starter, the main interactive phases, a plenary and a short close.
Here is a model for a 55 minute lesson.
• Starter: 5 to 8 minutes. Wake up the class and link to the last lesson.
• Main phase 1, Input: 10 to 12 minutes. Students meet the new language or skill in a text, an audio or a model.
• Main phase 2, Guided practice: 10 to 12 minutes. Students practise with support, often in pairs.
• Main phase 3, Free production: 12 to 15 minutes. Students use the language in a speaking or writing task of their own.
• Plenary: 5 to 8 minutes. Check learning against the objective.
• Close: 1 to 2 minutes. Homework and a clear sentence about the next lesson.

b: For a 40 minute lesson: shorten each phase, keep the plenary.
For a double lesson of 90 minutes: repeat the main phases twice with a short break.
If the class is slow, cut free production to a shorter task, not the plenary.

img.alt: A timeline bar showing a 55 minute lesson split into starter, input, guided practice, free production and plenary
img.cap: A 55 minute lesson: starter, three main phases and a plenary. The times can move, but the order helps students.

p: The starter has four jobs. It gets students into English. It recalls the last lesson. It prepares the mind for today's topic. It shows you who is ready.
A good starter is short, easy to explain, and needs little preparation. It should be active and use English. It should never be the same every day.
Examples (more in Unit 25):
• Show a picture and ask students to write five words about it in one minute.
• Put three true or false statements about last lesson on the board.
• Write a jumbled sentence for students to put in order.
Do not start with a long talk from the teacher. Students should be doing something in the first minute.

b: Is it short?
Does it use English?
Does it link to the objective?
Can I run it with no extra material?

p: In the input phase students meet the new skill, text or language. Your aim is understanding, not perfection.
Examples of input:
• A reading text, with a quick task to find the main idea.
• An audio clip, played twice, with a short listening task.
• A model answer, such as a good email, with the features underlined.
• A short talk by you, with a few questions to check.
Tips:
• Give a task before students read or listen. This gives them a reason.
• Keep teacher talk short. Show, do not tell.
• Check meaning with simple questions, not 'Do you understand?'.
• Let students compare answers in pairs before whole class feedback.

ex.t: Check meaning in a better way
b: Poor: 'Do you understand?'
Better: 'Show me with your fingers: is the answer one, two or three?'
Better: 'Tell your partner what the writer wants.'

p: In guided practice students use the new language with support. The task is controlled. There is a clear right answer or model, so students can succeed.
Examples:
• Gap fill and matching exercises.
• Making sentences from prompts.
• Pair drills with a model dialogue.
• Rewriting a paragraph with better linking words.
Walk around and listen. Do not sit at your desk. Note common errors on a small piece of paper for feedback later. Help only when needed. Keep praise specific: 'Good, you used 'although' correctly.'
Aim for a mix of interaction patterns: students working alone for one to two minutes, then pairs, then groups of three or four, then whole class.

b: Individual: thinking time.
Pair: more talk for every student.
Group: ideas and roles.
Whole class: sharing and feedback.

p: In free production students use the language to do a real task. They choose their own words. This is the phase where fluency grows.
Examples:
• A short talk on a Part 2 style card.
• A group discussion with a Part 3 question.
• Writing an email or a report from a stimulus.
• A role play at a shop or a help desk.

Give clear instructions, then step back. Write the timing on the board. During the task, do not correct every mistake. Listen and collect. After the task give feedback on three to five key language points, good and bad.
This phase is where students get most speaking and writing time. If you must shorten the lesson, shorten the earlier phases, not this one.

b: Say them once, in short sentences.
Show an example.
Check with one question: 'What are you going to do first?'
Start the timer.

p: The plenary brings the lesson back to the objective. It is not a goodbye. It is the moment when you and your students see what was learned.
Good plenaries:
• Students say or write one new thing they can now do.
• A quick quiz of three questions.
• A 'traffic light' check: green (I can do it), amber (I need practice), red (I need help).
• Students read a sentence they wrote today.
Use what you learn. If most students show red or amber, change tomorrow's plan. Write a short note in your lesson record. A plenary you ignore wastes time.

b: Look back at the objective. Did most students reach it?
What will I change tomorrow?
Who needs extra help?

p: Copy this template. Fill it in for every lesson. After some weeks you will not need to write everything, but the thinking should stay.
• Class, date and lesson number.
• Topic and syllabus skill codes.
• Lesson objective and two success criteria.
• Prior knowledge: what do they already know?
• Materials: texts, audio, cards, board work, technology and backup.
• Stages table: time, stage, teacher activity, student activity, interaction pattern.
• Possible problems and my plan for them.
• Differentiation: support, core and stretch tasks.
• Assessment: how I will check learning.
• Homework.
• After the lesson: what went well, what to change.

b: 0 to 6: Starter. Teacher shows picture. Students write words. Individual then pair.
6 to 18: Input. Teacher reads model email. Students underline. Pairs.
18 to 30: Guided practice. Students match openings and endings. Pairs.
30 to 45: Free production. Students plan and write. Individual.
45 to 53: Plenary. Students check with a checklist. Pairs.
53 to 55: Close. Homework.

sections.h: A full sample lesson: an informal email about a problem
p: Here is a complete 55 minute lesson, written for this course. It practises Paper 1, Exercise 5. A task like this appears in the 2024 specimen paper, where students write an email to a friend about a problem with something they bought online.

Objective: Students can write an informal email that explains why they bought something, describes a problem and says what they will do. Skill codes W1, W2, W4. Success criteria: I covered all three bullet points. I used friendly language. I linked ideas with 'so', 'because' and 'but'.
Materials: model email on paper, task sheet, checklist, a timer.
Starter (0 to 6 minutes): Students write the names of three things they bought online or in a shop and one problem each. Pair share.

Input (6 to 16 minutes): Read a model email. Students underline friendly phrases (Guess what! You won't believe this) and linking words. Answer three questions: Why did the writer buy it? What is the problem? What will the writer do?
Guided practice (16 to 28 minutes): Students match sentence openings to endings; rewrite three formal sentences in a friendly way (I would like to inform you becomes Guess what!).

Free production (28 to 45 minutes): Read the task: You recently bought an item online. There was a problem with it. Write an email to a friend. Explain why you bought the item, describe the problem, say what you are going to do. Write about 120 to 160 words. Students plan three paragraphs in two minutes, then write for 12 minutes.
Plenary (45 to 53 minutes): Swap emails. Use a checklist: Did the writer cover three points? Is it friendly? Are there linking words? Give two stars and a wish.
Close (53 to 55 minutes): Homework: improve the email using your partner's wish.
Differentiation: support with sentence starters; core with the checklist; stretch with a challenge to use two less common phrases.

b: Students see a model before writing.
They practise the language in small steps first.
They write for a real reader.
They check their work with a clear tool.

units.activity: Write a 55 minute lesson plan for one skill from Paper 1 or Paper 3. Use the template. Include a starter, three main phases, a plenary and a differentiation note. Teach it, then write three lines about what you would change.

check.q: About how long should the free production phase last in a 55 minute lesson?
Which is the main purpose of a plenary?
o: To give out the homework only
To check learning against the lesson objective

check.q: If a lesson is running late, what should you shorten?
o: The earlier phases, not the free production or plenary

units.title: Starters, Plenaries and Quick Checks
units.summary: Build a bank of twelve starters and ten plenaries, learn how to check understanding during the lesson, and set up vocabulary routines that keep new words alive.

p: A starter is the first activity. It should take five to eight minutes. Use these rules.
• It uses English from the first second.
• It needs very little preparation.
• It links to the last lesson or to today's topic.
• It is active: students write, speak, move or decide.
• It changes. Use different starters each week.
• It tells you something: who is ready, who forgot the last lesson?
Keep a list of starters on one page. Choose one in two minutes when you plan.

b: Teacher talks for five minutes about the topic: not a good starter.
Students match five words to pictures in pairs: good.
Teacher asks 'What did we do yesterday?' and waits in silence: weak.
A quick quiz with three questions on last week's grammar: good.

sections.h: Twelve starters you can use tomorrow
p: Here are twelve starters. Each one is quick and needs little material.
• 1. Word race: write as many words as possible on a topic in one minute (for example, kinds of homes).
• 2. Odd one out: show four words. Which does not belong? Students explain.
• 3. True or false: three statements about last lesson. Students decide and correct the false ones.
• 4. Picture prompt: show a picture. Students write five questions about it.
• 5. Quick-fire questions: ask five personal questions fast, students answer with a full sentence.
• 6. Jumbled sentence: write the words in the wrong order; students put them right.
• 7. Mini dictation: read two sentences slowly; students write them; pairs check.
• 8. Two truths and a lie: students write three sentences about themselves; partner guesses the lie.
• 9. Spelling relay: teams send one student at a time to write a word on the board.
• 10. One-minute talk: students talk to a partner on a simple topic without stopping.
• 11. Error hunt: write a sentence with one mistake from last lesson; students find it.
• 12. Question of the day: a big question on the board; students write one sentence answer and hold it up.

b: Speaking: 5, 8, 10, 12.
Writing: 1, 4, 6, 7.
Reading and vocabulary: 2, 9.
Review: 3, 11.

p: A plenary ends the lesson. It shows what students can now do. Here are ten plenaries.
• 1. Exit ticket: each student writes one thing they learned and one question on a slip of paper.
• 2. 3-2-1: three things I learned, two things I liked, one question.
• 3. Traffic lights: students hold up green, amber or red for the objective.
• 4. One sentence: write one sentence using today's language.
• 5. Teach your partner: explain one thing from today in 30 seconds.
• 6. Quick quiz: five questions on mini whiteboards or scrap paper.
• 7. Muddiest point: write the part that is still not clear.
• 8. Summary in ten words: students sum up the lesson in ten words.
• 9. Exam link: write one exam-style question about today's topic.
• 10. Self-check against success criteria: tick the criteria met.

ex.t: What to do with the slips
b: Sort them into three piles: got it, nearly, not yet.
Start tomorrow with a short review for the 'not yet' pile.
Keep a tally in your notebook.

p: Checking is not asking 'Do you understand?' Students nearly always say yes, even when they do not.
Use these tools:
• Concept checking questions (CCQs): simple questions that test meaning. For 'although', ask: 'Is it a reason or a contrast?'
• Instruction checking questions (ICQs): ask 'What do you do first?' after you give instructions.
• Mini whiteboards or paper: all students write an answer and hold it up together.
• Show with fingers: choose 1, 2 or 3.
• Wait time: after a question, wait three to five seconds before you choose someone. More students think.
• Ask students to explain to a partner before answering the class.
• Cold calling: choose a student by name after the question, not before, so everyone thinks.

b: Word: 'unusual'. Is it common or not common? Give an example.
Structure: 'I used to play football.' Do I play now?
Instruction: 'Work in pairs. One speaks, one listens.' Who speaks first?

p: A check is useful only if you act on it. Make a habit of three small steps.
• Note: write a quick note after each lesson. For example: 'Class 10B. Most used because correctly. Five students mix up take place and take part.'
• Adjust: change tomorrow's starter or first task to deal with the problem.
• Share: tell the students what you learned from their work. Say 'Most of you can... Some of you need...'.
Keep a one-page tracker for each class with the objective and a tick, a half-tick or a cross. At the end of the month you will see patterns.

b: Date | Objective | Evidence | Next step.
Example: 12 March | Use 'because' to give a reason | 20 of 28 students did it | Practise in the starter on Friday.

p: Vocabulary is a big part of the language marks in writing and speaking. Students must use a range of common and less common words. Words are forgotten quickly unless they come back many times.
Try these routines:
• Five new words per lesson, not more. Teach them in a sentence, not alone.
• Teach collocations: words that go together, such as 'make a decision', 'heavy rain', 'take part in'.
• Word families: teach 'decide, decision, decisive'.
• Word notebooks: students write the word, a sentence, the meaning and a translation if they need it.
• Spaced review: revisit new words after one day, one week and one month.
• Use words in speaking and writing tasks the same week.
Common words the examiner report says students mix up: 'take place' and 'take part'. Teach pairs like these together with examples.

b: Monday: teach five words.
Tuesday: starter quiz on the words.
Next Monday: use them in a short writing task.
One month later: a mixed review.

o: Read them only at the end of term
Throw them away after the lesson
Sort them and plan the next lesson from them
Mark every one with a grade

units.title: Integrating Skills: From Input to Output
units.summary: Learn how to join reading and listening to writing and speaking in one sequence, with four patterns, worked examples from the 2024 specimen paper and a weekly planning grid.

p: Receptive skills are reading and listening. Students take in language. Productive skills are writing and speaking. Students make language.

In the real world, we rarely use just one skill. We read an email and reply. We listen to a talk and discuss it. The Cambridge exam follows this idea. The papers test each skill alone, but the topics are real and the tasks link to real life.
When you link skills in one lesson sequence:
• Students have ideas and words to use when they speak or write.
• They see how language works in a real text first, then use it.
• They practise the same words and structures many times.
• You save time, because one topic serves four skills.
Without input, students often have nothing to say or write. Without output, they only recognise language and cannot use it.

b: Input first, then notice, then practise, then produce.
Always end with an output task.

sections.h: The skills chain: input, noticing, practice, output
p: Use this chain to plan a sequence of one to four lessons.
• Input: students read a text or listen to a recording. The first task is about meaning only. For example: What is the main idea?
• Noticing: students look closely at the language. Which words and phrases help? How is the text organised?
• Practice: students use the key language in controlled tasks with a correct answer.
• Output: students speak or write on a new but related topic, using the language they noticed.
• Feedback and redo: the teacher gives feedback and students try again.

b: Does the sequence start with input?
Is there a pause to notice language?
Do students get to produce something of their own?
Is there time for feedback and a second try?

img.alt: A diagram showing four steps in a row: input, noticing, practice, output, with an arrow back to feedback
img.cap: The skills chain. Input leads to noticing, practice and output. Feedback closes the loop.

sections.h: Pattern 1: Reading, then speaking, then writing
p: Here is an example using the reading text from the 2024 specimen Paper 1. The article, All about living stone plants, is about plants that look like small stones. It uses words such as resemble, tap root, container, sandy soil and protect.

Lesson A (reading). Students answer Exercise 1 questions. They find facts: where the plants grow, what the head is, how tall they are, what advice the writer gives. Task: underline the advice sentences.

Noticing. Look at how the text gives advice: 'it is best to grow them in sandy soil', 'it is important to protect the plants', 'it is essential to be patient'. These are patterns: it is + adjective + to + verb.
Lesson B (speaking). Pairs give advice about a plant or pet using the same pattern. Then a one-minute talk: 'Tell me about an animal or plant in your area and how to look after it.'
Lesson C (writing). Write an informal email to a friend who wants to grow a plant. Give three pieces of advice. 120 to 160 words.
Result: one text supports reading, speaking and writing, and students practise a useful structure in all three.

b: Take any short text from a past paper.
Pick one language pattern in it.
Plan one speaking task and one writing task that use the pattern.

sections.h: Pattern 2: Listening, then speaking, then writing
p: Pick a recording on a topic of the unit. It can be a Paper 2 extract, or a short recording you make yourself with a colleague.
Step 1: Listen for gist. What is it about? Who is speaking?
Step 2: Listen again for detail. Fill in a table or notes.
Step 3: Notice useful phrases. For example 'I'd rather', 'What I like about it is', 'In my opinion'.
Step 4: Speak. Pairs give their own opinion on the same topic using two of the phrases.
Step 5: Write. Students write a short summary or an email to a friend about what they heard and what they think.

Tip for Paper 2: after the exam practice, replay the recording with the script. Students see where the answers were and which words were distractors. The examiner report says many students pick the word they hear in the recording instead of the idea.

b: Recording: 'I suddenly heard a bang in the engine.'
Correct option: 'It made a loud noise.'
Many students did not link the two ideas.
Class task: match recording sentences to option sentences with different words.

p: Speaking can prepare writing. Talk first, write second. Students who have said their ideas aloud write more and with less fear.
Example: Paper 3 Part 2 card, 'School newspaper'. Students prepare for one minute, talk for two minutes in pairs about which article they would prefer to write and why.

Then switch to writing: write a short article or review about the same topic for the school newspaper. Use ideas from the talk. Students can listen to a partner's talk and take notes, then write an email to a friend about what the partner said.
This pattern also helps students who think they have nothing to write. They already said it.

b: Talk for one minute with a partner.
Write three key ideas from the talk.
Write a paragraph for each idea.

sections.h: Pattern 4: Reading two texts, then writing a report
p: Exercise 6 asks for a more formal piece, such as a report, article, review or essay. Students need ideas and a formal register. One good way is to give them two short texts with different views.
Step 1: Read text A (advantages) and text B (disadvantages). Underline key ideas.
Step 2: Notice formal phrases: 'It is clear that', 'However', 'On the other hand', 'In conclusion'.
Step 3: Plan: introduction, two paragraphs, a conclusion and a recommendation.
Step 4: Write 120 to 160 words, using ideas from the texts and one idea of your own.
Examiner reports remind us that students who only copy the prompts score lower for Content. They must develop prompts or add their own ideas.

b: The aim of this report is to...
One enjoyable part was...
However, there were some problems...
I would recommend that...

sections.h: A weekly planning grid for integrated skills
p: Use a grid to plan the week around one theme. Here is an example for the theme 'Travel'.
• Lesson 1: Reading. A short article on a travel problem. Exercise 1 and Exercise 3 skills. Notice linking words.
• Lesson 2: Listening. Two short travel stories. Exercise 2 style. Notice phrases for opinions.
• Lesson 3: Speaking. A Part 2 style card: a train journey or a bus journey. Talk for two minutes. Peer feedback.
• Lesson 4: Writing. An email to a friend about a journey, 120 to 160 words, using ideas and phrases from Lessons 1 to 3. Feedback and redo.
Check: in four lessons you practised all four skills, used the same topic words and finished with one piece of real output.

b: Too much input and no time for output.
Skills that are not connected to the same topic.
Giving the same task every week.
No feedback loop, so students repeat the same mistakes.

Which skills are receptive?

units.title: Teaching with Past Papers and the Specimen Paper
units.summary: Use past papers and the 2024 specimen Paper 1 in lessons, with the full structure of the specimen paper, its answers and practical three-lesson sequences for each exercise.

sections.h: When and how to use past papers
p: Past papers are the best practice for the exam because the questions match the real style. But they are not the best first step. Use them in stages.
• Stage 1: Learn the task. Look at one exercise, learn what it asks, practise the skill with easier texts.
• Stage 2: Practise by exercise. Do one exercise at a time with time limits.
• Stage 3: Timed full paper. Do a whole paper under exam rules, once or twice a term.
• Stage 4: Review and redo. Go through the mark scheme, find errors and try again.
Do not give a past paper every week from the start. Students become afraid, and teachers miss the chance to build skills. Use mock exams at the end of modules and in the final term.
Keep the real mark scheme. After every attempt, ask students to mark their own or a partner's work with the mark scheme. This is excellent training.

b: June 2024 papers and mark schemes (download).
The 2024 specimen Paper 1 and mark scheme (download).
Older papers for your syllabus period: ask the School Support Hub.
Never share live exam papers or confidential materials.

p: The specimen paper shows the structure for examination from 2024. It has 17 questions and 60 marks. Use it to explain the paper to students.
• Exercise 1 (Questions 1 to 6, 8 marks). A short article, All about living stone plants. Five one-mark questions and one three-mark question (advice).
• Exercise 2 (Question 7(a) to (i), 9 marks). A matching task with nine statements.
• Exercise 3 (Questions 8 and 9, 7 marks). Notes under two headings about tiny homes: three marks for disadvantages and four marks for reasons they are popular.
• Exercise 4 (Questions 10 to 15, 6 marks). Six multiple-choice questions, three options each.
• Exercise 5 (Question 16, 15 marks). An informal email to a friend about a problem with an item bought online. Three bullet points. About 120 to 160 words. 6 marks Content, 9 marks Language.

• Exercise 6 (Question 17, 15 marks). A report about a sports festival, using speech-bubble comments as ideas and also some ideas of your own. About 120 to 160 words. 6 marks Content, 9 marks Language.

b: Reading: 8 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 30 marks.
Writing: 15 + 15 = 30 marks.
Total: 60 marks.

sections.h: The specimen answers, and how to teach from them
p: Here are the answers from the specimen mark scheme, with teaching ideas.

Exercise 1. Q1 South Africa. Q2 (the) head. Q3 prevents insect attacks. Q4 mist. Q5 two centimetres. Q6, any three of: grow them in sandy soil, protect the plants from strong sunlight, use a container of sufficient depth, be patient.
Teaching idea: ask students to highlight the key word in each question before they read ('country', 'pair of leaves', 'protect', 'main source of water', 'how tall'). Then let them find the sentence.

Exercise 2. Q7: (a) C, (b) A, (c) D, (d) B, (e) C, (f) D, (g) B, (h) A, (i) D. Teaching idea: students underline the key words in the statement, then find the idea in the texts. They must find paraphrase, not the same word.

Exercise 3. Q8 disadvantages of tiny homes, any three: high cost of the fuel needed to transport them; not every region has building regulations; not always straightforward to connect to a range of services; can be tricky to control the temperature inside. Q9 reasons why they are popular, any four: can be easily moved; encourages you to get rid of unnecessary possessions; increased media interest in the idea; many companies now specialise in building them; desire to leave a smaller carbon footprint.
Teaching idea: notes should be short and under the right heading. Practise by sorting notes into 'disadvantages' and 'reasons for popularity'.
Exercise 4. Q10 A, Q11 C, Q12 B, Q13 A, Q14 B, Q15 B. Teaching idea: for each option, ask students to find the sentence in the text that matches or rejects it. Only one fully answers the question.

b: Brackets in the mark scheme mean the words are not essential.
One mark for each acceptable detail up to the maximum.
Spelling errors in reading answers do not lose marks if the meaning is clear and unambiguous.
Marks are never taken away for errors or for omissions.

p: Exercise 5, Question 16. The task: You recently bought an item online. There was a problem with it. Write an email to a friend about the problem. In your email you should explain why you bought the item, describe the problem with the item and say what you are going to do about it. Write about 120 to 160 words.

Use the three bullets as a plan: paragraph 1 why I bought it, paragraph 2 the problem, paragraph 3 what I will do. Add a greeting and a friendly ending. Use informal language: contractions, exclamations, questions to the reader.

Exercise 6, Question 17. The task: Your class took part in a one-day sports festival. The organisers want students' opinions. Write a report saying what was enjoyable and suggesting how it could be improved. Comments from students: 'It was a chance to meet students from other schools', 'There weren't many new sports to try', 'I learned a lot about fitness', 'We spent too much time listening to instructions.'

Plan: introduction (aim of the report), what was enjoyable, what could be improved with suggestions, a conclusion. Use a formal or semi-formal style. Use some of the comments and add ideas of your own.
Both tasks are marked with Table A (Content, 6 marks) and Table B (Language, 9 marks), which you studied in Week 2.

b: Address all three bullets in Exercise 5 to reach the higher marks.
In Exercise 6, extend or add to the prompts.
Keep the register right: friendly for the email, formal for the report.
Do not confuse 'take place' with 'take part'.

sections.h: A three-lesson sequence for one exercise
p: Use this pattern for any exercise.
Lesson A: Learn the task.
• Show the exercise. Ask: What do I have to do? How many marks? How long should I take?
• Do a similar short task with an easier text together.
• Teach the strategy (for example, underline key words, find paraphrase).
Lesson B: Practise.
• Students do the real exercise in a set time, alone.
• Mark in pairs with the mark scheme.
• Collect common errors.
Lesson C: Review and redo.
• Talk through the hard questions and why wrong options look good.
• Students correct errors and write an error log.
• A short second attempt on a new text or new question.

b: Question number | My answer | Correct answer | Why I got it wrong | What I will do next time.
Review the log before the next mock exam.

p: A full mock gives you and your students real information.
• Plan the date in your calendar.
• Use a quiet room, desks apart, no dictionaries, clock visible.
• Give instructions exactly as in the exam: read the instructions, do all questions, write on the paper.
• Time it. Paper 1 takes 2 hours.
• Mark all papers using the mark scheme. Use the Content and Language tables for writing.
• Give feedback within a week. If you wait a month, the lesson is lost.
After the mock, plan three lessons for the three most common problems. Do not move on to a new topic before you reteach.
Balance: past papers should be only part of your course. Keep using texts and recordings from outside the exam too, so students read and listen for real.

b: Group the common errors.
Reteach in a new starter or a small-group lesson.
Praise students who improved.
Set one target for each student.

sections.h: Try your plan with a colleague
p: Plans are better when someone else reads them. Ask a colleague to read your lesson plan and answer three questions.
• Could I teach from this?
• What will the students be doing in minute 20?
• How will you know if the objective was reached?

If possible, invite the colleague to observe part of the lesson. After the lesson, talk for 10 minutes. Start with what went well. Then choose one thing to change. Observation is not a test. It is a way for both teachers to learn.

b: Time | What students were doing | What I noticed.
Write facts, not opinions.

p: Next week you will go deeper into how you teach. You will learn about communicative language teaching and task-based learning. You will also learn how to make your own reading, writing and speaking tasks, and how to adapt textbooks and create simple checklists for students.

units.title: Communicative Language Teaching: Getting Students Talking
units.summary: Learn what communicative language teaching (CLT) is, how to increase Student Talking Time (STT), which activity types get students speaking, how to manage group work and how to correct errors well.

sections.h: Welcome to Week 5: how you teach
p: In Week 4 you planned your lessons. This week you look at the way you teach them. Good plans fail if students do not get a chance to use English. The aim of this week is simple: more student talk, better tasks and better resources.
This week you will learn:
• Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) and how to use it.
• Task-Based Learning (TBL) and how to run a task cycle.
• How to teach speaking for Paper 3.
• How to make your own reading, speaking and writing tasks.
• How to adapt endorsed textbooks safely.
• How to build checklists so students can check their own progress.

b: Bring one real text from a newspaper or website.
Think of one class where students are quiet. Why?

p: CLT is a way of teaching where students learn English by using it to communicate. The main goal is that students can use the language in real situations. It is not only learning rules.
Key ideas of CLT:
• Meaning comes first. Students use the language to do something real: ask, explain, agree, decide.
• Fluency and accuracy both matter. Fluency means communicating without long stops. Accuracy means using correct grammar and words.
• Students work together in pairs and groups. They are not only listeners.
• The teacher is a guide, not only a speaker. The teacher plans the task, listens and helps.
• Language is learned in context, with real or realistic topics.
• Errors are normal. They show that learning is happening.
Myths about CLT:
• 'CLT means no grammar.' Not true. Grammar is taught, but through use.
• 'CLT is only speaking.' Not true. Reading and writing tasks can be communicative too.
• 'CLT is noisy and out of control.' It can be well organised, with clear tasks and time limits.

b: Students fill in gaps with the correct verb: not very communicative.
Students interview each other and note answers: communicative.
Students read a text and then decide with a partner which advice is best: communicative.
Students copy sentences from the board: not communicative.

sections.h: Student Talking Time and Teacher Talking Time
p: Student Talking Time (STT) is the time students spend speaking English. Teacher Talking Time (TTT) is the time the teacher speaks. Many trainers suggest that in a speaking lesson students should speak for at least half of the time, and much more in some activities. The Cambridge Speaking test is only 10 to 15 minutes, but the practice takes many hours.
Why STT matters:
• Students learn to speak by speaking.
• They try new words and see what works.
• They get ready for Paper 3, where they must talk for two minutes alone.
How to measure STT:
• Ask a colleague to watch a lesson and tick every time a student speaks and when the teacher speaks.
• Record 10 minutes on a phone and listen. Count how many students speak.
• Count how many different students speak, not only how long.
Teacher talk is not bad. Clear instructions, good models and feedback are needed. But the teacher should speak only when it helps learning.

b: Who spoke most in the last 10 minutes: me or my students?
How many students did not speak at all?
What could I change to give them more time?

sections.h: Ten ways to increase Student Talking Time
p: Try these ideas.
• 1. Pair work first. In a class of 40 students, pair work gives 20 speakers at once.
• 2. Think, pair, share. Students think alone for 30 seconds, tell a partner, then share with the class.
• 3. Give wait time. Wait three to five seconds after a question.
• 4. Short instructions. Say them once, show an example and check with one question.
• 5. Ask open questions. 'Why do you think that?' is better than 'Is it true?'.
• 6. Do not repeat or rephrase every answer. Let students listen to each other.
• 7. Use roles in groups: speaker, note-taker, timekeeper, reporter.
• 8. Use mingle activities. Students walk around and speak to many partners.
• 9. Use a 'three before me' rule. Students ask three classmates before asking the teacher.
• 10. Put students in rows or circles that help them face each other.

b: Use pairs and rows, not whole class questions.
Teach students signals for starting and stopping.
Use the same pair activities every week so students know the routine.

sections.h: CLT activity types for IGCSE ESL
p: Here are common CLT activities with examples that match the exam.

• Information gap: each student has different information and must ask questions. Example: Student A has the morning timetable of a school trip, Student B has the afternoon. They ask and complete the full timetable.
• Opinion gap: students give their own opinion and may disagree. Example: 'Should students wear a uniform?' Tell your partner your view and one reason.
• Reasoning gap: students decide between options and explain. Example: Choose the best gift for a friend from five options. This links to Paper 3 Part 2.
• Role play: students act a situation. Example: ask for a refund for a product with a problem.
• Jigsaw: each student reads a different part of a text and tells the others.
• Survey or mingle: students ask the same question to many people and record the answers.
• Problem solving: groups plan a school event with a budget.
• Discussion with roles: one student chairs, one summarises, others give views.

b: Student A: You know the cost of a theatre trip and the time. Ask B about the museum trip.
Student B: You know the cost of a museum trip and the time. Ask A about the theatre trip.
Then decide together: which trip is better value, and why?

p: Group work can go wrong if it is not planned. These steps help.
• Give a clear task and outcome. Say what students must produce.
• Set a time and show a timer.
• Make groups of two to four. Larger groups mean fewer speakers.
• Give roles when needed.
• Mix levels for helping, or group by level for challenge. Change groups often.
• Move around the room. Listen. Do not sit.
• For early finishers, have an extension: 'Now tell your partner two reasons to disagree.'

• For students who share a first language: ask them to use English for the task, and agree rules. If they must use the first language to understand, allow it for ten seconds and then return to English.
• For shy students: give them time to prepare notes, work in pairs first, and praise effort.

b: Task, outcome and time are clear.
Roles are given.
I have a plan for early finishers.
I will listen and collect errors.

p: Monitoring means walking around and listening while students work. You have three jobs: help, listen and collect.
• Help: answer a question or give a word. Keep it short.
• Listen: notice good language and errors. Write down five examples on paper.
• Collect: do not interrupt the task for every error.
Correct in the right moment. When the task is about fluency (such as a discussion), delay correction. Wait until the end.
Delayed correction method:
• Write 5 to 6 sentences from students on the board without names. Include both good sentences and sentences with errors.
• Ask the class to find and fix the errors in pairs.
• Praise a student who said something good.

In accuracy practice, correct more quickly. Use techniques such as: repeating the sentence with a questioning tone, using fingers to show word order, giving a hint ('past tense?'), or asking a peer to help.
Do not correct everything. Choose errors that block understanding or that appear again and again. This matches the exam, where marking credits what students can do.

b: Student said: 'I really wanted to take place in the event.'
Better: 'take part in the event.'
Student said: 'Yesterday I go to the shop.'
Better: 'Yesterday I went to the shop.'

p: Some teachers worry that CLT will not prepare students for the exam. In fact the exam rewards communication. The Speaking test is a real conversation, and writing marks go to clear, developed content. The examiner report for June 2024 says strong responses are well developed, use a range of structures and vocabulary, and have clear organisation.
A balanced week might be:
• Two lessons of communicative tasks, with a focus on talk and writing.
• One lesson of exam skills with past paper exercises.
• One lesson of language focus and feedback.
This way students get both fluency and exam technique.

b: Communicative tasks: about half of the time.
Exam skills: about a quarter.
Language focus and feedback: about a quarter.

units.title: Task-Based Learning: The Willis Framework and a Full Lesson
units.summary: Understand task-based learning (TBL), follow the Willis framework of pre-task, task cycle and language focus, study a complete speaking lesson and a writing lesson, and compare TBL with PPP.

p: In task-based learning (TBL), students learn English by doing tasks. A task is a piece of work where students use English to reach a real outcome. They focus mainly on meaning. They use their own words.
A real task has:
• A clear goal or outcome, such as a list, a decision, a plan or a short talk.
• A reason to communicate.
• A gap: something students need to find out, decide or create.
• Meaning first, with language support second.
Examples of tasks:
• Choose the best place for a class trip and tell the class why.
• Make a list of ten rules for a school club.
• Solve a problem: you have missed the last bus. What can you do?
• Plan a school event with a budget and present it.

b: Fill the gaps with the correct preposition: exercise.
Decide with a partner which of two options is better and explain why: task.
Write the past tense of ten verbs: exercise.
Prepare a one-minute talk on a hobby and give it to a partner: task.

p: Jane Willis described a well-known TBL framework in her 1996 book A Framework for Task-Based Learning. It has three stages: pre-task, task cycle and language focus.
• Pre-task: The teacher introduces the topic and the task. Students recall words they know. The teacher may play a recording of others doing the task. Time: 5 to 10 minutes.

• Task cycle: This has three parts. First, the task: students do it in pairs or groups while the teacher monitors and does not correct. Second, planning: students prepare to report to the class what they did or decided. They ask the teacher for help with language. Third, report: students present or exchange their written work, and the class compares results.

• Language focus: Students look at the language of the task. First analysis: find and discuss useful words and structures in a text or recording. Then practice: the teacher leads exercises on useful words and patterns. Time: 10 to 15 minutes.

b: Students use language first, then study it.
The teacher focuses on form after the task, based on what students needed.
The report stage gives a real audience.

img.alt: A flow diagram of the task-based learning framework: pre-task, task cycle with task, planning and report, then language focus
img.cap: The Willis task-based learning framework: pre-task, task cycle (task, planning, report) and language focus.

sections.h: A full TBL speaking lesson: the school trip decision
p: This lesson practises Paper 3 Part 2 skills: comparing two options and saying which one you prefer. It lasts about 60 minutes.

Pre-task (10 minutes). The teacher shows pictures of a museum and a national park. Students brainstorm words: exhibition, guide, tickets, hiking, wildlife, view. The teacher plays or reads a short model talk of a student comparing two options, and students note phrases such as 'On the one hand' and 'I would rather'.

Task (10 minutes). In groups of three, students decide which trip the class should take. Each says one advantage and one disadvantage of each option. The group must reach a decision and prepare two reasons.
Planning (8 minutes). Each group prepares to report. They write key words, not a script. The teacher helps with language but does not correct mistakes in the discussion.
Report (10 minutes). Each group tells the class its decision in 30 to 60 seconds. The class votes on the best reasons.

Language focus (15 minutes). The teacher writes sentences from the task on the board, good and with errors. Students find and fix the mistakes. They underline phrases for comparing and preferring. Then they practise in pairs with new options (a concert or a football match).
Follow-up: each student records a two-minute talk at home on a new card.

ex.t: Why this lesson works for Paper 3
b: Students meet comparison language before they need it.
They do the task twice: in the group and again in the report.
The teacher uses real errors from the lesson.
The follow-up copies the real exam talk.

sections.h: A TBL writing lesson: a short report
p: TBL works for writing too. Here is a 60 minute lesson for a report on a school event.

Pre-task (10 minutes). Show headings of a report: Introduction, What was good, What could be better, Conclusion. Students read a short model and underline useful phrases. Brainstorm: what words can we use for 'good' and 'bad'?
Task (15 minutes). In groups of three, students list what was good and what could be improved at a real school event (sports day, assembly, exam week). They choose three ideas and write notes.
Planning (10 minutes). Each group plans a short report in four paragraphs. They decide who writes which paragraph and help each other with language.
Report (10 minutes). Groups exchange drafts. Readers underline two good phrases and one thing to improve.

Language focus (15 minutes). The teacher shows frequent errors and phrases that make the report formal ('It would be helpful if...', 'I would suggest that...'). Students correct and rewrite. For homework, each writes a 120 to 160 word report on their own, based on the group notes.

b: Students share ideas in a group.
They write alone for the exam style.
They get feedback twice: from peers and from the teacher.

p: PPP stands for Presentation, Practice, Production. The teacher presents a language item (such as the past simple), students practise it in controlled exercises, then produce it in a freer task. TBL changes the order: students try the task first, then focus on language.
PPP strengths:
• Clear, simple to plan.
• Good for beginners and for specific grammar.
• Students feel safe because they know what to say.
TBL strengths:
• More real communication and talk.
• Students use their own words and show what they already can do.
• Language teaching follows student needs.
TBL challenges:
• Needs more careful task design.
• Can be harder to manage in large classes.
• Students who like clear rules may feel unsure at first.

A good plan for the exam class: use both. Use PPP for a clear structure that students often get wrong (for example conditionals or the passive). Use TBL to build confidence and fluency, as in Paper 3.

b: Students never use the past tense in speaking: short PPP then a TBL task.
Students are shy and use short answers: TBL with pair tasks.
Students need a model of an email: present a model and practise, then produce.

p: Use this checklist to build your own tasks.
• Does the task have a clear outcome (list, plan, decision, talk)?
• Do students have a reason to talk (a gap or a choice)?
• Is the level right? A little challenging but possible.
• Is there a time limit?
• Is there a topic that students know or care about?
• Can the teacher see the result?
• Is there a chance to report to others?
Types of tasks:
• Listing: brainstorm and make a list.
• Ordering and sorting: put items in order or in categories.
• Comparing: find similarities and differences.
• Problem solving: find a solution.
• Sharing personal experience: tell stories.
• Creative tasks: write a poster, a quiz or a short play.

b: Students finish too early: add a second stage or a harder question.
Students use their first language: give a reward for English and give a role to each student.
Weak students stay silent: pair with a patient partner and give sentence starters.
The teacher worries about grammar: plan the language focus for the end.

p: Link every task to an exam skill. For Paper 3: Part 1 tasks are personal interviews, Part 2 tasks are comparison talks and Part 3 tasks are opinion discussions. For Paper 1: writing tasks are emails and reports.
A termly plan could be:
• Weeks 1 to 4: TBL tasks based on Part 1 type questions (personal topics).
• Weeks 5 to 8: TBL tasks based on Part 2 cards (two options).
• Weeks 9 to 12: TBL tasks based on Part 3 questions (opinions and discussion).
Keep timing in mind. Students must prepare for one minute and talk for up to two minutes in Part 2, so practise this exactly in the report stage sometimes.

b: Does my task have an outcome?
Does it prepare for an exam task?
Will I give feedback after?
