units.title: Teaching Speaking for Paper 3
units.summary: Use the June 2024 teacher's notes and the examiner report to teach speaking for Paper 3: the test format, what strong and weak talk sounds like, a language bank, practice routines and a mock speaking day.

p: Paper 3 is worth 40 marks and takes about 10 to 15 minutes per student. It is done in English, recorded in full and marked by the teacher. Students speak to the teacher or examiner alone.
The parts and times (from the June 2024 teacher's notes):
• Introduction: about 1 minute. Not assessed.
• Warm-up: 1 to 2 minutes. Not assessed.
• Part 1, Interview: 2 to 3 minutes. Assessed. Three questions on one topic.
• Part 2, Short talk: 3 to 4 minutes, including 1 minute to prepare. The student talks alone for up to two minutes about the card. Assessed.
• Part 3, Discussion: 3 to 4 minutes. Assessed. Questions linked to the Part 2 topic.
The marks are 10 each for Grammar, Vocabulary, Development and Pronunciation, applied across all three parts.

b: No notes in the room and no dictionaries.
They may ask for clarification at any time.
The examiner chooses the card, not the student.
They get a card only for Part 2.

sections.h: What the teacher's notes tell us
p: The 2024 teacher's notes contain ten Speaking Assessments, A to J. Each has a warm-up, a Part 1 topic with three questions, a Part 2 card with two options, and Part 3 questions.

Topics in the series (Part 1 topic and Part 2 card): cooking and inventions; staying healthy and a school newspaper; being helpful and a holiday abroad; your local area and a sports event; jobs and listening to music; art and giving a presentation; clothes and being environmentally friendly; animals and ways of learning; popular music and lifestyle; free-time activities and studying a story.
Look at the pattern of the three Part 1 questions:
• Question 1 asks about now or habits: 'Can you tell me something about the food you usually eat at home?'
• Question 2 asks for a past story: 'Can you tell me about a time when ... and what happened?'
• Question 3 asks for an opinion: 'Do you think ... ? Why? Why not?'

The Part 2 card always gives two options and asks students to compare and say which they prefer and why. The tasks use different focus: how useful, how easy or difficult, how enjoyable, the advantages and disadvantages.
Part 3 questions are opinion questions on a wider theme, such as 'Do you agree...?' or 'What are the advantages and disadvantages of...?'
Keep these notes confidential for the live series. Use your own cards that follow the same pattern for class practice.

b: Give students a past topic and ask them to predict the three Part 1 questions.
Check against the pattern: now, past, opinion.

sections.h: What strong and weak talk sounds like
p: The June 2024 examiner report for Speaking gives clear pictures. Here is a summary in simple words.
Strong Part 1 answers:
• Use the right tense for each question: present for habits, past tenses for a past event, future or 'should' for opinions.
• Use a range of simple and complex structures, such as modals, conditionals and comparatives.
• Give examples and details.
Weak Part 1 answers:
• Stay in the present tense for a past story.
• Give one or two short sentences and repeat words from the question.
Strong Part 2 talks:
• Start with a short introduction and say how the talk will be organised.
• Talk about both options, with advantages and disadvantages.
• Use linking words to move between ideas and finish with a clear preference and a reason.
Weak Part 2 talks:
• Talk about only one option.
• List only advantages for both.
• Do not say which option they prefer.
Strong Part 3 answers:
• Develop ideas with precise vocabulary and examples.
• Refer back to earlier points.
Weak Part 3 answers:
• Give relevant but very short answers with simple words.
The report also says many students did not give a past story when asked, so listen carefully to the tense of each question.

b: Listen to the tense in the question and answer in the same time.
Talk about both options.
Say which you prefer, and why.
Keep talking for the whole two minutes.

p: Give students phrases they can use. They need to practise until they are natural.
Starting the talk (signposting):
• 'I'm going to talk about two options: ... and ...'
• 'Both options have advantages and disadvantages, so let me start with...'
Comparing:
• 'On the one hand... on the other hand...'
• 'Compared with..., ... is more...'
• 'The main difference is that...'
Giving reasons and examples:
• 'because', 'since', 'so', 'which means that', 'for example', 'for instance'.
Giving an opinion:
• 'In my opinion', 'I believe', 'I'd say that', 'To be honest'.
Speculating and conditionals:
• 'If I went to..., I would...', 'It might be...', 'I suppose that...'
Past stories:
• 'It was last year when...', 'I was walking when...', 'I had never seen...', 'I used to...'
Buying time:
• 'Let me think...', 'That's an interesting question.', 'What I mean is...'
Finishing:
• 'So, overall I would choose... because...', 'In the end, I prefer...'

b: Give each student a card with a phrase and a task.
Students use the phrase in a one-minute talk.
The partner tallies each time it is used.

p: Plan short activities for each criterion.
Grammar (10 marks)
• Practise the tense that goes with each question type.
• Do short drills: change present to past, make conditional sentences, add a relative clause.
• Encourage complex structures (conditionals, relative clauses, passive) but do not make students afraid of mistakes.
Vocabulary (10 marks)
• Teach topic sets (health, travel, work, environment, technology).
• Teach collocations and phrasal verbs.
• Aim for precise words, not only fancy words. 'Infuriating' is better than 'annoying' only if it fits.
Development (10 marks)
• Teach the pattern: point, reason, example.
• Use extension prompts: 'Can you tell me more?', 'Why?', 'Can you give an example?'
• Practise talking for two minutes without stopping.
Pronunciation (10 marks)
• Work on clear sounds, word stress and sentence stress.
• Teach intonation: rising and falling to show meaning and feeling.
• Record students and let them listen to themselves.
Remember that pronunciation is its own criterion. A student with simple grammar can still have clear pronunciation and earn marks for it.

b: Tongue twisters for sounds.
Minimal pairs for confusing sounds.
Read a sentence five ways to show five feelings.
Underline stressed words in a paragraph and read it aloud.

p: Short, regular practice beats one long mock.
• Starter (5 minutes, every lesson): a Part 1 question. Pairs ask and answer. Rotate question types: now, past, opinion.
• Midweek (15 minutes): one Part 2 card. One minute to prepare, then partners talk for two minutes each while a third student times and listens.
• End of week (15 minutes): Part 3 questions in groups of four with a chair and a note-taker.
• Monthly: a recorded talk to listen to and mark with the four criteria.
Use a visible timer. Students must feel two minutes. Many students speak for only 45 seconds the first time.
Use your own cards. Write new ones each month. Use topics from the students' real life.

b: 30 seconds: say it once.
One minute: say it with a reason.
Two minutes: say it with a reason, an example and a comparison.

p: A mock before the real test builds confidence. Plan it like the real thing.
• Choose a quiet room and test the recording device.
• Prepare cards for Part 2 and question lists for Part 1 and Part 3.
• Start the recording with your name, the student's number and name, and the date, as in the real test.
• Use the scripts from the teacher's notes.
• Time each part. Do not let a student run beyond the time.
• Follow the prompts in the notes if a student does not start or stops early.
• Mark with the four criteria. Use best fit and decide the level and then the mark within the level.
• Listen again to a sample with a colleague and compare.
Marking problems found in the June 2024 examiner report:
• Some centres were generous when students spoke naturally but used a narrow range of structures.
• Some marked severely because of accent when the pronunciation was clear.
• Many did not mark pronunciation on its own evidence.
• Some marked for quantity of speech even when the answer was not relevant.

b: Give each student two strengths and one target.
Plan a lesson for the common weaknesses.
Keep the recordings to compare progress.

sections.h: Supporting students who find speaking hard
p: Some students are shy. Some have a small vocabulary. Others get nervous. Help them in steps.
• Start with pair work, then groups, then the teacher.
• Give sentence starters for the first minute.
• Let them rehearse with a partner before speaking in front of the class.
• Use recordings at home so they can listen and try again.
• Praise effort and clear sounds, not only perfect grammar.
• Show them that mistakes do not stop communication.
• Teach them to ask for clarification, which is allowed in the test: 'Could you repeat that, please?'
For stronger students: ask them to include a conditional, to give a surprising example, or to challenge a partner's idea politely.

b: Support: sentence starters and prepared notes in the practice stage.
Core: a card and a timer.
Stretch: two complex structures and an extra example.

units.activity: Write your own Part 2 card in the Cambridge style with two options and a task sentence. Test it with two students. Record one talk. Mark it with the four criteria and list two strengths and one target.

check.q: What does Part 2 of Paper 3 require the student to do?
o: Discuss a picture with a partner
Answer three questions about a topic
Talk alone about two options on a card and say which they prefer and why

check.q: What is the main problem with weak Part 2 talks according to the examiner report?
o: They use too many linking words
They focus on only one option or do not state a preference

check.q: How many marks are given for Pronunciation?

units.title: Creating Reading Worksheets: From Real Text to Cambridge-Style Tasks
units.summary: Learn how to choose a real text and turn it into tasks like Exercises 1 to 4, with rules for good questions, a full worked example, a quality checklist and a way to test your worksheet.

sections.h: Why make your own reading tasks
p: Past papers are limited. You may use them all in one term. Students also need practice with topics that matter in their own lives. When you make tasks yourself, you can use local topics, current news and your students' level.
The key is to copy the Cambridge style so the practice matches the exam. This unit shows how.
Remember what the exam looks like (from Week 1):
• Exercise 1: a text of about 400 to 450 words. Six questions, short answers, last question asks for three details. 8 marks.
• Exercise 2: matching, a text of about 600 to 650 words in up to five sections, or up to five shorter texts. Nine questions. 9 marks.
• Exercise 3: notes completion from a text of about 400 to 500 words. 7 marks.
• Exercise 4: multiple choice, a text of about 550 to 600 words, six questions with options A, B, C. 6 marks.

b: Practice for topics you want to review.
A chance to bring local examples into the class.
A way to adjust difficulty for your students.
A model for students who later write their own questions.

p: Look for texts that students would actually read, and that are connected to the exam topics: technology, health, travel, environment, school life, jobs, hobbies, culture and festivals.
Where to look:
• Newspaper and magazine articles for young readers.
• Websites about science, nature or travel.
• School newsletters or notices.
• Your own writing. You can write a text for your class in 20 minutes.
How to check the text:
• Level: students should understand most words (about 90 to 95 percent) at a normal reading speed. A few new words should be guessable from context.
• Length: choose the length for the exercise, or use a shorter text for a first practice.
• Content: facts, opinions and details that give you good questions.
• Topic: respectful, clear and not too sensitive.
• Names, dates and numbers: not too many, unless you want them for questions.
Copyright: use short extracts for classroom teaching, name the source, and do not publish the text. If in doubt, write your own text or ask the author.

b: Can I write six good questions about it?
Are there ideas that can be paraphrased?
Is it too easy or too hard?
Is it safe and fair for my class?

p: Exercise 1 asks short answers. The answers are single words or short phrases from the text.
Rules for writing questions:
• Write five questions with one answer, and one question that needs three details.
• Put questions in the same order as the information in the text.
• Ask who, what, where, when, how and why. Avoid questions with 'yes' or 'no'.
• Make sure there is only one possible answer.
• Make questions use different words from the text to test understanding.
• Choose answers of one to four words.
Mark scheme tips:
• Write the correct answer and other acceptable answers.
• Use brackets for words that are not needed: '(the) head'.
• For the three-detail question, give four or five possible details so that students can choose any three.
The examiner report warns students not to add wrong information, and to be precise. For example, a question about the title of an event needs the key word 'World' in 'World Cosplay Summit'.

ex.t: A weak and a strong question
b: Weak: 'Is the plant easy to grow?' (yes or no).
Strong: 'What is the main source of water for plants without a long root?'

p: Exercise 2 asks students to match nine statements to sections of text or short texts.
Rules:
• Use up to five short texts or sections, A to E.
• Write nine statements. Each answer is one of the texts. Some texts can be used more than once.
• Write each statement using paraphrase, so students must understand meaning, not match words.
• Include some statements that test implied meaning, such as 'which person suggests...'.
• Make sure only one text fully fits each statement.
• Avoid giving the same exact words as the text.

The examiner report for June 2024 says students find it hard when the key word of the statement is 'suggests', or when two texts contain the same word. Your task should train students to read the whole paragraph and follow the discourse markers (but, however, although, because).

b: Text: 'I'll turn up whatever the weather, however cold or wet.'
Statement: 'Which person says they will go swimming whatever the weather?'

p: Exercise 3 asks students to complete notes under headings. Answers are short notes, not full sentences.
Rules:
• Choose a text with a list of ideas or two clear groups (for example, advantages and disadvantages).
• Write a heading and a note frame with a space for the answer.
• Say how many notes are needed: 'Give three points'.
• Make sure the heading controls what the answer must be. The notes must fit the heading, as the examiner report says.
• Write the answers in brief form, with a verb after the heading when the heading needs it.
Example heading: 'Ways cities can reduce traffic' and the note: 'charging drivers to enter parts of the city'. A note that says only 'charging drivers' lacks key meaning.
Mark scheme: list all acceptable notes and mark the essential words in capitals so markers can see what is needed.

b: Heading: Reasons people like tiny homes.
1 ______ (they can be moved easily).
2 ______ (people can get rid of things they do not need).

sections.h: Step 5: Write Exercise 4 style multiple choice
p: Exercise 4 has six multiple-choice questions with options A, B and C.
Rules:
• Write the stem as a clear question or an unfinished sentence.
• Write one correct option that fully answers the question.
• Write two distractors. Each distractor should be mentioned in the text but should not answer the question.
• Make the options the same length and grammar.
• Do not write 'all of the above' or 'none of the above'.
• Put the correct answer in different positions.
• Include one or two questions about implied meaning or the writer's opinion. Use words like 'suggests' or 'implies' in the stem.
How to check: ask a colleague to answer without the text. If they can guess the answer, the options are too obvious.
The examiner report says students often pick an option because one word matches the text. Plan distractors that use text words but give the wrong idea.

b: Stem: What does the writer suggest about people who cycle to work?
A They save money on fuel.
B They arrive at work earlier.
C They are healthier than drivers.
Only one is supported by the whole paragraph.

sections.h: A worked example: an original text and six questions
p: Here is a short text written for this course. It is shorter than an exam text. Use it to see the rules in action.

Text: The Return of the Bicycle. Twenty years ago, many cities were full of cars. Streets were noisy, the air was dirty and traffic moved slowly. Today, things are changing in some places. In a city called Riverton, the government built a network of safe cycle lanes. At first, many people said nobody would use them. However, within two years, the number of people riding to work had doubled. Shop owners were worried that customers would stop coming, but sales went up because people stopped to look in the windows. The city now plans to add 50 kilometres of new lanes by 2030. Not everyone is happy. Some drivers say the lanes make the roads too narrow. Even so, a recent survey found that three out of four residents support the plan.
Questions:
• 1. What was the problem in cities twenty years ago? (Answer: (too many) cars / traffic.)
• 2. What did the government of Riverton build? (Answer: (a network of) safe cycle lanes.)
• 3. How long did it take for the number of cyclists to double? (Answer: (within) two years.)
• 4. What did shop owners fear? (Answer: customers would stop coming.)
• 5. What is the plan for 2030? (Answer: 50 (kilometres) of new lanes.)

• 6. Give three details about how people feel about the lanes. (Answers: at first people said nobody would use them; shop owners worried; some drivers say roads are too narrow; three out of four residents support the plan.)

b: Questions are in the order of the text.
Answers are short.
There is one clear answer for each.
The last question gives four possible details for three marks.

sections.h: Quality checks before you use the worksheet
p: Always test your worksheet.
• Do it yourself without looking at your key. Do you get the same answers?
• Ask a colleague to do it. Where do they hesitate?
• Time it. Is it realistic for the lesson?
• Check each question: could there be two correct answers? Fix the question or add the second answer to the key.
• Write the key with acceptable alternatives and marks.
• Label each question with a skill code: R1 facts, R2 connections between ideas, R3 selecting details, R4 implied meaning.
• Print clearly, with a title and instructions in the same style as the exam.
After use, check the results. If most students miss one question, look at the question before blaming the students. Maybe it was unclear. Improve the worksheet and save the new version.

b: Add a pre-reading question to get students ready.
Add a post-reading task: 'Do you agree with the writer?'
Create two versions: a support one with glossary and a stretch one with an extra open question.

units.activity: Take the real text you brought. Choose one exercise type, write six or nine questions and the key. Swap with a colleague. Have them answer without your key and tell you where the questions were unclear. Improve your worksheet.

check.q: What should the options in a multiple-choice question be like?
o: One correct option and two distractors of similar length that are mentioned in the text

check.q: What is the best way to test your own worksheet?
o: Give it to the whole class without checking
Ask a colleague to do it and note where they hesitate

check.q: Why should a mark scheme show brackets, such as '(the) head'?
o: To show the order of questions
To show the answer is wrong
To show words that are not essential for the mark

units.title: Creating Speaking and Writing Prompts
units.summary: Write your own Paper 3 interview questions, Part 2 cards and Part 3 discussion questions, and your own Exercise 5 and Exercise 6 writing tasks, using the real patterns and a quality checklist.

p: Cambridge changes the cards and tasks each year. Students need many different practice prompts. When you write your own, you can match topics to your students' lives and you can practise each skill again and again.
A good prompt does four jobs:
• It is clear. Students know what to do.
• It is fair. It does not need special knowledge.
• It is open. It lets students say a lot.
• It matches the exam pattern. Students learn what to expect.

b: Read three real examples carefully.
Notice the exact wording.
Copy the pattern, not the words.

sections.h: Part 1 interview questions: the three-question pattern
p: Each Part 1 topic has three questions. They follow a pattern.
• Question 1: now or habits. 'Can you tell me something about...?' or 'How do you...?'
• Question 2: a past story. 'Can you tell me about a time when..., and what happened?'
• Question 3: an opinion or the future. 'Do you think...? Why? Why not?'
Original examples:

• Festivals: 1 What festivals do you celebrate with your family? 2 Can you tell me about a festival you enjoyed, and what happened? 3 Do you think festivals are important for a community? Why? Why not?
• Transport: 1 How do you usually travel in your town? 2 Can you tell me about a time when your journey went wrong, and what happened? 3 Do you think cities should have fewer cars? Why? Why not?

• Shopping: 1 Where do you usually buy your clothes? 2 Can you tell me about something you bought that you were happy with? 3 Do you think young people spend too much money on things they do not need? Why? Why not?
• School clubs: 1 Which clubs does your school have? 2 Can you tell me about a time when you took part in a club activity? 3 Should every student join a club? Why? Why not?
Keep the language simple. Avoid words that need special knowledge.

b: Choose a topic: music, pets, technology, weather, the internet, volunteering.
Write Q1 now, Q2 past, Q3 opinion.
Ask a student to answer and note if the tenses are used.

p: The card has a title, a context sentence, two options in bullet points and a task. The task asks students to talk about the options and say which one they prefer and why. The questions focus on how useful, how easy or difficult, how enjoyable, or the advantages and disadvantages.
Template:
• Title (two or three words).
• Context: 'Your school is planning a... You are considering the following options:'
• Option 1.
• Option 2.
• Task: 'Talk about how ... each option would be. Say which option you would prefer, and why.'
Original examples:

• Card 1: Learning a skill. Your friend wants to learn a new skill during the holidays. You are considering the following options: joining a cooking class; learning to play the guitar. Talk about how difficult each option would be. Say which option you would prefer, and why.

• Card 2: A school trip. Your class is planning a trip. You are considering the following options: visiting a science museum; spending a day at the beach. Talk about the advantages and disadvantages of each option. Say which option you would prefer, and why.

• Card 3: Helping at home. You want to help your family more. You are considering the following options: doing the cooking once a week; looking after your younger brother or sister after school. Talk about how easy or difficult each option would be. Say which option you would prefer, and why.

• Card 4: Keeping in touch. A friend has moved to another country. You are considering the following ways to stay in touch: sending messages every day; making a video call once a week. Talk about how useful each option would be. Say which option you would prefer, and why.

b: The two options are both realistic and equally easy to talk about.
There is no right answer.
The task words match the options (advantage, difficulty, enjoyment, usefulness).
The language level is easy to read in one minute.

p: Part 3 asks four or more questions connected to the Part 2 topic but wider. They ask for opinions and reasons. They often start with 'Do you think...', 'Some people say... What is your opinion?', 'Do you agree?' or 'What are the advantages and disadvantages of...?'
Original examples for the card 'A school trip':
• Some people say that school trips are a waste of time. What do you think?
• Do you think students learn more outside the classroom than inside? Why? Why not?
• What are the advantages and disadvantages of travelling in a large group?
• All students should visit a different country before they leave school. Do you agree?
Tips:
• Do not repeat what was in the card. Move to a larger idea.
• Mix agree/disagree statements with open questions.
• Make sure students of any background can answer.

b: Write four Part 3 questions for each of your four cards.
Try them with two students.
Which questions gave the longest answers?

sections.h: Writing tasks for Exercise 5: the informal email
p: Exercise 5 gives a situation, an instruction to write an email to a friend, three bullet points, and the word limit. The pattern from the 2024 specimen paper is:
• Situation: one or two sentences.
• Instruction: 'Write an email to a friend about...'.
• 'In your email you should:' with three bullet points.
• 'Write about 120 to 160 words.'
• 'You will receive up to 6 marks for the content of your email, and up to 9 marks for the language used.'
Original examples:
• You recently went to a concert. Write an email to a friend about it. Say why you went, describe what you saw and heard, and say if you would go again.
• You have started learning a new sport. Write an email to a friend about it. Explain why you chose the sport, describe your first lesson and say what you hope to achieve.
• Your school has a new student from another country. Write an email to a friend about the new student. Describe the student, say how you welcomed them and say what you plan to do together.
The bullets should cover: a reason, a description and a plan or a feeling. Make each bullet one clear task.

b: Is the reader a friend?
Are there exactly three bullets?
Is each bullet clear and possible to develop?
Is the word limit stated?

sections.h: Writing tasks for Exercise 6: formal writing with stimulus
p: Exercise 6 is a more formal piece. It may ask for an article, report, essay or review. It gives a situation, an instruction, a stimulus such as speech bubbles, and a request to use some of the ideas and add ideas of your own.

The 2024 specimen Question 17 shows this pattern: a class took part in a one-day sports festival. Students wrote a report that said what was enjoyable and suggested improvements, using four comments in speech bubbles.
Original examples:

• Report: Your school held a careers day. The organisers want students' opinions. Say what was useful and how it could be improved. Comments: 'I met people from different jobs'; 'The talks were too short'; 'There were not enough students at the talks'; 'I learned how to write a CV'.
• Article: Write an article for your school magazine about why young people should learn to cook. Comments: 'It saves money'; 'It is healthier'; 'It can be a fun hobby'; 'It takes too much time'.

• Review: Write a review of a film, book or app you recently tried. Say what was good, what was less good and whether you would recommend it. Comments: 'The story was exciting'; 'It was too long'; 'The pictures were beautiful'; 'It helped me practise English'.
• Essay: 'Students should be allowed to use phones in class.' Comments: 'Phones are useful for research'; 'They can distract students'; 'Some students have no phone'; 'Teachers should decide'.
Always ask for 120 to 160 words and give the marks for Content and Language.

b: Is the audience clear (organisers, readers, a teacher)?
Do the comments give ideas that can be extended?
Does the task need students to add their own ideas?
Is the register formal or semi-formal?

p: Once you have prompts, use them in different ways.
• Pair practice: one student asks, one answers, then swap.
• Speaking stations: set up three places with different cards. Students rotate every three minutes.
• Write after talk: students talk about the card, then write the same ideas as a report.
• Peer test: a student acts as the examiner and the partner takes the test. The third student marks with a checklist.
• Prompt bank: store them in a folder labelled by topic and level. Add a note about which worked best.
Share prompts with colleagues. Ask for new ideas each term. Keep a master copy with answers or sample responses.

b: Topic | Part 1 questions | Part 2 card | Part 3 questions | Writing task | Notes.
Add 3 new prompts every month.

units.activity: Write one complete speaking set (three Part 1 questions, one Part 2 card, four Part 3 questions) and one Exercise 5 email task and one Exercise 6 task. Test the speaking set with a student and the writing tasks with a colleague. Note what to improve.

check.q: What kind of question is Question 2 in a Part 1 set?
o: A question about a past event
A question about the present only

check.q: What should an Exercise 5 task have?
o: A formal letter and no bullets
A situation, an email to a friend and three bullet points

check.q: What is true of a good Part 2 card?
o: It has two realistic options and asks for a preference with a reason

units.title: Adapting Endorsed Materials: Scaffold, Stretch and Use Safely
units.summary: Learn what endorsed textbooks are, how to judge a textbook activity, five moves to adapt it, how to scaffold and extend, a worked example and how to use publishers' books within copyright rules.

p: Endorsed materials are books and resources that Cambridge has checked and approved as a good match for a syllabus. Publishers such as Cambridge University Press and Collins make them. They usually include a student's book, a workbook, a teacher's guide and audio.

For example, the Collins Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language Student's Book, third edition, is endorsed for examination from 2024. Always check the Cambridge website for the current list of endorsed resources for your syllabus year.
What endorsement means:
• The book follows the syllabus and the exam style.
• Cambridge has looked at the quality of the content.
What it does not mean:
• It does not mean the book is perfect for your class.
• It does not mean you must use every page.
• It does not replace the syllabus, the past papers or the mark schemes. The syllabus is always the main document.

b: Use the contents page to match units to your scheme of work.
Use the teacher's guide for ideas and keys.
Use the audio scripts after listening tasks.

sections.h: How to judge a textbook activity
p: Before you use an activity, ask these questions.
• Syllabus fit: which skill code does it practise (R1, W2, L2, S3)?
• Level: is it too easy or too hard for my class?
• Time: can I do it in the lesson?
• Interest: is the topic close to my students' life?
• Interaction: do students talk or write, or only fill gaps?
• Support: are there models, word lists, answers?
• Gaps: what is missing, such as speaking practice or feedback?
Give each activity a quick score: keep, change or skip.

b: A gap-fill on the past tense: keep but add a speaking task after it.
A very long reading with hard vocabulary: change by splitting it into two parts with a glossary.
A discussion topic that your students do not know: swap it for a local topic.

sections.h: Five moves to adapt an activity
p: There are five easy moves. Remember them as the five S's.
• Select: choose only the activities you need.
• Swap: change names, places and topics for local ones.
• Scaffold: add support so that more students can succeed.
• Stretch: add challenge for stronger students.
• Supplement: add a speaking or writing task, or a quick check, that the book does not give.

b: Which pages will I select?
What will I swap?
How will I scaffold?
How will I stretch?
What will I supplement?

p: To scaffold means to give temporary support, like the frame around a building. Remove it when students can work alone.
Ways to scaffold:
• Pre-teach key words before reading or listening.
• Give a model answer or a first example.
• Give sentence starters for speaking and writing.
• Divide a long task into small steps.
• Give a graphic organiser, such as a table or a spider diagram.
• Let students read or listen twice and compare answers in pairs.
• Offer hints or partly completed answers.
• Use pictures.
• Pair a stronger student with a student who needs support.
• Allow extra time.
Scaffolds should help students think, not give them the answers.

ex.t: A scaffold for a short talk
b: I'm going to talk about two options: ___ and ___.
The main advantage of ___ is that ___.
However, ___ because ___.
So overall I would choose ___ because ___.

p: Strong students need challenge too. Ways to stretch:
• Add an open question after a closed one: 'Why do you think the writer chose these words?'
• Ask for two or three reasons instead of one.
• Remove support, such as the word list or the model.
• Ask students to write their own questions about a text for a partner.
• Ask students to rewrite for a different audience (for example, a formal letter instead of an email).
• Add a time limit.
• Ask them to compare two texts.
• Ask them to give a short talk using the same material.

b: After a reading task, students write three questions for the next class.
After a listening task, students write a short email answering the speaker.

sections.h: A worked example of adapting one task
p: Imagine a textbook page with a reading about public transport and these tasks: read the text; answer six questions; discuss the question 'Do you use public transport?'
The class has mixed levels and little speaking practice. Here is how you could adapt.
• Select: keep the reading and the six questions.
• Swap: add a local bus route as a second short text.
• Scaffold: pre-teach six key words (commute, fare, ticket, platform, delay, schedule) and let students read twice and compare answers in pairs.
• Stretch: ask stronger students to write two more questions for a partner and to find the writer's opinion.

• Supplement: turn the discussion into a Part 2 style card: 'You are choosing between a bus and a bicycle to get to school. Talk about how useful each option would be. Say which you would prefer, and why.'
Result: the same page now gives reading practice, vocabulary, speaking and a clear exam link.

b: Planning: about 20 minutes.
Preparing a glossary and a card: 10 minutes.
The result can be reused every year.

p: Textbooks and audio are protected by copyright. Respect it to protect authors and to keep your school safe.
• Read your school's licence and the publisher's terms. They may allow limited copying for classroom use.
• Do not copy whole books or share them online.
• Do not post audio or scripts in public places.
• When you adapt, make your own new version, not a copy of the publisher's pages.
• Always write the source on worksheets (for example, 'Adapted from ...').
• Use free official resources from Cambridge, such as past papers and the examiner reports on the Cambridge website, as they allow.
• Keep confidential exam materials, such as live speaking cards, secure.
If you are unsure, ask your head of department or the publisher.

b: Do I have permission to copy?
Is my version new and different?
Is the source written down?
Is anything confidential?

sections.h: Mapping a book to your scheme of work
p: Use your four-column scheme to plan with the book. Put the unit pages into Column 2 and Column 3. Then look for gaps.
• Does the book give enough practice for Paper 3 Part 2 and Part 3?
• Is there enough exam-style writing?
• Are there enough listening tasks of the Cambridge style?
• Are mark schemes or criteria included?
Add your own tasks to fill the gaps. Cross out the activities you will skip. Share the map with colleagues so everyone teaches the course in the same way.

b: Unit | Pages | Syllabus skill | Keep, change or skip | My addition.

units.activity: Choose one page from a textbook or a past paper. Judge it with the seven questions. Then adapt it with the five S's, write the changes and use it in class. Note what happened.

units.title: Formative Checkpoints: Peer and Self-Assessment Checklists
units.summary: Build simple, student-friendly checklists from the official Cambridge criteria for writing, speaking, reading and listening, and teach students to use them for peer and self-assessment.

sections.h: Why students should check their own work
p: Formative assessment means checking learning while it happens, so it can still be improved. Students who learn to check their own work become independent learners. They understand what a good answer looks like. They find their own mistakes. They know what to practise next.
Cambridge speaks of learners who reflect, and teachers who build practice from reflection. A checklist is a small, simple tool for this.
Benefits:
• Students understand the marking criteria in plain words.
• Feedback arrives sooner, not weeks later.
• You mark less, because students fix many errors first.
• Students feel responsible for their progress.

b: It is not a test or a grade.
It is not a list of every grammar rule.
It is a small number of clear questions for one task.

p: Use these rules.
• Base it on the official criteria. For writing: Table A Content and Table B Language. For speaking: Grammar, Vocabulary, Development, Pronunciation.
• Use simple words and 'I' statements: 'I covered all three bullet points.'
• Keep it short: five to eight items.
• Make each item easy to answer yes or no, or with a traffic light.
• Link to action: after the check, students must fix one thing or set one target.
• Update the checklist when students are ready for the next step.
• Teach students how to use it. Use it first on a sample, not on their own work.

b: Green: I did this well.
Amber: I did this a little.
Red: I did not do this.
Choose one red or amber item to improve first.

p: Here is a checklist based on the Content table (task fulfilment and development of ideas) and the Language table (range, accuracy and organisation).
Content:
• I answered all three bullet points.
• Everything I wrote is about the task.
• I used a friendly style, like talking to a friend.
• I added reasons, details or examples.
Language:
• I used different words, not the same word again and again.
• I tried some longer sentences with 'because', 'although' or 'which'.
• I checked my verbs and tenses.
• I used linking words such as 'first', 'then', 'so' and 'but'.
• My email has a short start and a short ending.
Length:
• I wrote about 120 to 160 words.
Final step: choose one thing to improve and rewrite one sentence.

b: Do not use very formal expressions in an email to a friend.
Do not confuse 'take place' and 'take part'.
Keep the tenses clear and do not mix past and present by mistake.

sections.h: Checklist 2: Exercise 6, the report, article, review or essay
p: Content:
• I used the type of text the task asked for (report, article, review or essay).
• I used some of the ideas in the prompts and developed them.
• I added at least one idea of my own.
• I wrote for the right reader in the right style (more formal).
• I did not copy the prompts word for word.
Language:
• I used a range of vocabulary, including some less common words.
• I used a range of structures, simple and complex.
• My paragraphs are in a clear order: introduction, main points, conclusion.
• I used linking words and phrases such as 'however', 'in addition' and 'for example'.
• My conclusion uses different words from my introduction.
Length:
• 120 to 160 words.
These match what the examiner report says: balanced comments, development of ideas and cohesion help students reach the higher levels.

b: Underline the idea you added yourself.
Circle three linking words.
Count the words.

p: Based on the four marking criteria. Students can use it after a practice talk with a partner or after listening to their own recording.
Grammar:
• I used the right tense for each question (present, past, future).
• I tried a longer structure, such as 'if ...' or 'which ...'.
• I corrected myself when I noticed a mistake.
Vocabulary:
• I used words that fit the topic.
• I used at least three new words or phrases from our lessons.
• I did not repeat the same word all the time.
Development:
• I gave a reason and an example for each answer.
• I talked about both options on the card.
• I said which option I prefer and why.
• I kept speaking until the end of the two minutes.
Pronunciation:
• My words were clear.
• I stressed the important words.
• My voice went up and down to show meaning.
For the peer: say two stars (two good things) and a wish (one thing to improve next time).

b: Level 3: I give simple answers and sometimes add a reason.
Level 4: I give relevant answers and mostly add reasons and examples.
Level 5: I give developed answers with a wide range of words and structures, and I speak with ease.

p: A reading checklist helps students use good strategies.
Before reading:
• I read the title, the pictures and the questions.
• I underlined the key words in each question.
While reading:
• I looked for the paragraph that matches each question.
• I read the whole paragraph, not only one sentence.
• I looked for the same idea in different words (paraphrase).
• I watched for words like 'however', 'but' and 'although' that change the meaning.
• For multiple choice I checked each option against the text.
After reading:
• My short answers are exact. I did not add extra wrong details.
• I checked my notes are under the right heading.
• I checked my spelling of the words I copied.

b: Which question was hardest?
Why did I miss it?
What will I try next time?

p: Listening is a skill where students cannot go back, but they hear each recording twice. A checklist helps them use both listening opportunities well.
Before listening:
• I read the questions and options.
• I predicted words I might hear.
First listening:
• I got the main idea and marked an answer.
Second listening:
• I checked my answers.
• I listened for the idea, not only the same words. I know the option may use different words from the recording.
• I paid attention to the speaker's voice and opinion.
After listening:
• I looked at the script and found where each answer was.
• I wrote the words I did not catch and practised them.

ex.t: A tip from the examiner report
b: Many errors come from choosing an option because a word was heard, not because the idea matched.
Practise matching ideas, not words.

p: Do not just hand out the checklist. Teach it in four steps.
• Model: use the checklist on a sample answer on the board, and think aloud.
• Practise together: students check a second sample in pairs, then compare with the teacher.
• Use on their own work: students check a draft and tick.
• Act on it: students make one change, then hand in the improved version.
Peer feedback tips:
• Start with two good things.
• Give one clear wish. Be kind and specific.
• Use the checklist words, not 'it is bad'.
• Do not give marks, only comments.
To avoid students ticking everything, ask them to show evidence: 'Underline the three linking words'.

b: Star 1: You used 'although' correctly.
Star 2: Your introduction is friendly.
Wish: Try to add a reason in the third paragraph.

p: Use a simple tracker so students can see growth.
• Skill tracker: a table with the skill codes (R1 to R4, W1 to W4, L1 to L4, S1 to S4 in your own words) and traffic lights each month.
• Targets: each student has one target for each month, for example 'use three linking words in every paragraph'.
• Portfolio: keep one piece of writing and one recorded talk each month. Compare them at the end of term.
• Review with the teacher: five minutes with each student each term to talk about the tracker.
Use the information. If most students are amber in W2, plan a lesson on linking. If most are green, move on. Share progress with students and parents in simple words.

b: Skill: Writing, organisation.
My target: use linking words.
How I will practise: check each email with the checklist.
Date to check: 30 November.

units.activity: Choose one skill. Build a student checklist of five to eight 'I' statements from the Cambridge criteria. Test it with a partner and a sample answer. Revise it. Then teach your students to use it with one piece of work and collect their feedback.

units.title: Course Wrap-Up: Your Learning Tracker, Action Plan and Final Assessment
units.summary: Update your KWL chart for Week 5, review your whole course portfolio, write a 90-day action plan, learn where to find more help and prepare for the final assessment.

sections.h: Your Week 5 entry and the whole-course reflection
p: Update the L column of your KWL chart for Week 5. Write at least two specific things you learned about teaching approaches and making resources.
Then look back at your very first K column from Week 1. Write one paragraph that answers three questions:
• What do I now know that I did not know before?
• What will I do differently in my classroom?
• What do I still want to learn?
Be specific. For example: 'I used to talk for most of the lesson. Now I plan pair tasks and I check Student Talking Time every week.'

b: Learned: TBL has three stages: pre-task, task cycle and language focus.
Learned: scaffold, stretch, swap, select and supplement when adapting a textbook.
Learned: student checklists should be short and use 'I' statements.
Question: how do I run speaking tests for a class of 45?

p: You have built many useful things across five weeks. Put them into one folder, on paper or on a computer, with a clear name for each.
• Week 1: a two-year outline and notes on entries and access arrangements.
• Week 2: a marking portfolio with sample marked answers, a speaking marking sheet and notes from the examiner reports.
• Week 3: a year map with an exam buffer, a scheme of work and a diagnostic test.
• Week 4: a four-column scheme for two weeks, a lesson plan, a bank of starters and plenaries, an integrated skills sequence and a past paper sequence.
• Week 5: a TBL lesson, a speaking set, writing tasks, a reading worksheet, an adapted textbook activity and student checklists.
Look at the folder. Where are the gaps? Make a list of three things to finish.

b: Is everything saved in one place?
Is each item named and dated?
Have I shared one item with a colleague?

p: A plan keeps you moving. Choose five or six actions, each with a date.
• Days 1 to 30: use your year map and diagnostic results to set up your classes. Teach three lessons from your new lesson plan. Start a tracker.
• Days 31 to 60: run a speaking mock, a reading worksheet, a writing task, and use checklists. Meet your colleague to review results.
• Days 61 to 90: run a short mock paper, mark with the mark scheme, plan reteaching and update your scheme of work.
Make each action SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Examples:
• By 15 November: teach one TBL lesson and note STT.
• By 30 November: build two student checklists and use them.
• By 15 December: run a mock speaking day with recordings.
• By 31 January: share my best three resources with the department.

b: Action | Why | When | Help needed | Done when.

p: Keep learning. Here are good places.

• The Cambridge School Support Hub: your school's Support Coordinator can give you access. Look in the Teaching and learning section of the syllabus page for teacher guides, schemes of work, past papers, examiner reports and training information.
• The Cambridge International website: syllabus, samples database and the Cambridge Handbook.
• Cambridge professional development: online, virtual and face-to-face courses for teachers.
• Endorsed resources from publishers: check the current list.
• A colleague or mentor: observe each other and talk about lessons.
• Teacher communities in your country or online: ask for ideas and share yours.
Plan a monthly meeting with one colleague to share one lesson idea and one problem.

b: Keep a one-page 'What I tried and what happened' record.
Review it each month.
Add one new idea each time.

p: The final assessment has 146 questions across all five weeks. You need 75 percent to pass and receive your certificate.
How to prepare:
• Review the key words at the top of each unit.
• Review the questions you missed in the unit practice checks.
• Review the tables: Paper 1, 2 and 3 marks and times, the Content and Language tables, the four speaking criteria.
• Review the planning ideas: year map, exam buffer, scheme of work, four columns, lesson structure, starters and plenaries.
• Review the teaching approaches: CLT, STT, TBL stages, scaffold and stretch, checklists.
In the assessment:
• Read each question and every option.
• Many questions use short classroom situations. Choose the best action.
• If you are unsure, remove options you know are wrong first.
• Check your time: take about a minute per question.

b: Teaching is a skill that grows with practice.
Small steps, repeated, make big changes.
Share what you learned with another teacher.

questions.q: About how many guided learning hours is the 0510 syllabus planned for?
questions.why: The syllabus is designed around about 130 guided learning hours, but this is only guidance.

questions.q: What does 'guided learning hours' mean?
o: Time spent in the exam hall only
Time a teacher spends teaching or guiding the student
Time a student spends on holiday

questions.q: In which exam series can students normally be entered?
questions.why: Students can be entered in June and November. Schools in India can also use March.

questions.q: Which extra series is open to schools in India?
questions.why: Schools in India can also enter candidates in the March series.

questions.q: Who sends the entries to Cambridge International?
questions.why: Exams officers are responsible for submitting entries.

questions.q: Why do Cambridge schools have an administrative zone?
o: Each zone has its own exam timetable and papers
questions.why: Papers and timetables are produced for different zones to keep exams secure.

questions.q: Which of these can a student take together with 0510 in the same series?
questions.why: Different subjects can be combined. The English-language syllabuses listed as exceptions cannot.

questions.q: Can students retake the qualification?
o: Only if they got grade G
Yes, as many times as they want
questions.why: Candidates can retake the whole qualification as many times as they want.

questions.q: What is true about Speaking tests from an earlier series?
o: They are deleted by Cambridge after one day
They can always be sent in again
Only the interview can be reused
They cannot be sent in again, in whole or in part
questions.why: Candidates cannot resubmit Speaking tests from a previous series.

questions.q: In which language are the syllabus and assessment materials available?
questions.why: This syllabus and its assessment materials are available in English only.

questions.q: What is an access arrangement?
o: A way to make the exam easier for everyone
A change that removes a barrier for a student with SEN, disability, illness or injury
questions.why: Access arrangements are reasonable adjustments that remove barriers without lowering the standard.

questions.q: When should a centre check which access arrangements are available?
o: At the start of the course
questions.why: Availability should be checked at the start of the course.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a condition for approving an access arrangement?
o: It does not harm the security of the assessment
It has a reasonable cost and timeframe
It makes the exam easier for the student
questions.why: Arrangements must be reasonable and must not weaken the exam. They are not meant to make it easier.

questions.q: What does the grade 'Ungraded' mean?
o: The work did not reach the standard for grade G
questions.why: Ungraded means the standard for grade G was not reached.

questions.q: Which letter on a statement of results means 'pending'?
questions.why: Q means pending. X means no result.

questions.q: How is Speaking reported where students reach the right standard?
o: Inside the A* to G grade
With the letters Q or X
questions.why: Speaking is separately endorsed with grades 1 to 5.

questions.q: Cambridge says grade C overall with Speaking grade 2 can be seen as roughly which CEFR level?
questions.why: The syllabus states this combination can be considered equivalent to B2.

questions.q: How long is Paper 1 Reading and Writing and how many marks does it have?
questions.why: Paper 1 is 2 hours and 60 marks.

questions.q: What share of the written grade is Paper 2 Listening?
questions.why: Listening is 30 per cent. Paper 1 is 70 per cent.

questions.q: Which statement about Paper 3 Speaking is correct?
o: It is internally assessed and externally moderated
It is marked only by Cambridge examiners
It is part of the written grade
questions.why: The teacher marks Speaking and Cambridge moderates the marks.

questions.q: Which assessment objective is about understanding implied meaning in reading?
questions.why: R4 is understanding implied meaning.

questions.q: Which writing objective is about the right register and style for the purpose and reader?
questions.why: W4 covers register and style.

questions.q: Reading quickly to get the general idea of a text is called:
questions.why: Skim reading means reading fast for the general idea.

questions.q: Which word shows contrast?
questions.why: Although, however, whereas and in contrast show contrast.

questions.q: Which text type is usually informal and published on a website?
questions.why: A blog is usually informal and published online.

questions.q: How many exercises are in Paper 1?
o: Four: two reading and two writing
Six: four reading and two writing
questions.why: Paper 1 has four reading and two writing exercises.

questions.q: How are the 15 marks for each writing exercise shared?
questions.why: Up to 6 for Content and up to 9 for Language.

questions.q: How many times do students hear each recording in Paper 2?
questions.why: Candidates hear each recording twice.

questions.q: In the Speaking test, which parts are assessed?
questions.why: Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3 are assessed. The introduction and warm-up are not.

questions.q: How is the Speaking test marked?
o: Four criteria (grammar, vocabulary, development, pronunciation) each out of 10
questions.why: Each of the four criteria has a maximum of 10 marks, giving 40 in total.

questions.q: Which statement matches the Cambridge marking principle about errors?
o: Marks are deducted for every error
Marks depend on the student's grade target
Marks are not deducted for errors or omissions
Half marks may be given for small errors
questions.why: Principle 3: marks are awarded positively and are not taken away for errors or omissions.

questions.q: Can an examiner give a half mark?
o: No, marks are always whole marks
questions.why: Principle 2: marks are always whole marks.

questions.q: In a mark scheme, text in brackets ( ) means the text:
o: may be included but is not essential
is worth a mark by itself
questions.why: The mark scheme says bracketed text may be included but is not essential.

questions.q: When marking with a level descriptor, work convincingly meets the level. Which mark do you give?
o: The lowest mark in the level
The highest mark in the level
questions.why: Convincingly meets the level means the top mark. Adequately means a middle mark. Just meets means the lowest mark.

questions.q: Why should examiners not think about grade thresholds while marking?
o: Marks are based only on the mark scheme requirements
questions.why: Principle 6: marks are based solely on the requirements in the mark scheme.

questions.q: In June 2024 Exercise 1, which answer earns the mark for 'When was the term cosplay invented?'
questions.why: The text says the activity started in 1939 but the name was created in 1984.

questions.q: What type of cosplay does Lana prefer?
questions.why: She likes science fiction but says fantasy is what she would choose first.

questions.q: Question 6 asks for three details and has three marks. A student writes five correct details. How many marks?
questions.why: The key says up to a maximum of three marks.

questions.q: Which of these is a POLICY introduced to reduce car use in the June 2024 article?
questions.why: Car-free zones is a policy. The other three are things the writer tried himself.

questions.q: Which answer is acceptable for Question 9, what the writer tried to reduce his own car use?
o: charging drivers to enter the city
questions.why: Sharing a car is something the writer did himself. The others are policies.

questions.q: How many marks are there in Exercise 3 (Questions 8 and 9)?
questions.why: Question 8 is 4 marks and Question 9 is 3 marks, so 7 in total.

questions.q: In the June 2024 wild swimming task, who is the best match for 'explains why they avoid saying where they swim' (7b)?
questions.why: Emine says regular swimmers value their private places.

questions.q: Who is the best match for 'mentions being surprised to see wildlife while swimming' (7d)?
questions.why: Ana describes a seal appearing next to her and says she did not expect it.

questions.q: Who is the best match for 'will go wild swimming whatever the weather' (7f)?
questions.why: Ana says it does not matter how cold or wet it is.

questions.q: In ToddlerLab, why is Serena asked to wear special gloves (Question 12)?
o: To make her fingers easier to see
So cameras can record her hand movements
questions.why: The gloves have reflective material so ceiling cameras can follow her hands.

questions.q: What does 'as she does so' refer to in ToddlerLab Question 15?
questions.why: It refers to running around the room, which is moving rapidly.

questions.q: How are the 15 marks shared in Paper 1 Exercises 5 and 6?
o: Up to 9 for Content and up to 6 for Language
Up to 6 for Content and up to 9 for Language
questions.why: Table A Content is up to 6 and Table B Language is up to 9.

questions.q: What does the Content table assess?
o: Task fulfilment and development of ideas
questions.why: Content covers task fulfilment (relevance, style, purpose and audience) and development of ideas.

questions.q: How many questions are there in Paper 2 Listening and how many marks?
questions.why: Paper 2 has 40 multiple-choice questions, each worth one mark.

questions.q: In the June 2024 Listening key, what is the answer to Question 27?
questions.why: Question 27 is in the multiple-matching exercise (Exercise 4) and the key gives G.

questions.q: Which three facts do you need before writing a two-year scheme of work?
o: Student names, school colours and room numbers
Grade boundaries, last year's marks and parents' jobs
Textbook prices, bus routes and holiday dates only
Guided learning hours, exam series and real teaching weeks
questions.why: These facts show how much time you really have and when the exam is.

questions.q: Why should you record mock exam marks by exercise as well as the total?
o: It shows which exercises and skills need reteaching
questions.why: Exercise-level records show where marks are lost.

questions.q: Roughly, how many guided learning hours does the syllabus plan for?
questions.why: The syllabus is designed around about 130 guided learning hours as guidance.

questions.q: Which Cambridge learner attribute is described as 'using a range of language to communicate ideas and information effectively in writing and speaking'?
questions.why: This is the description of the confident learner.

questions.q: Which route is most suitable first for a teacher who is new to Cambridge?
questions.why: Introductory training helps new teachers understand the syllabus and assessment.

questions.q: Where do Cambridge teachers find the Principal Examiner Report for Teachers and Results Analysis?
o: Cambridge support resources such as the School Support Hub
Only at the end of year concert
questions.why: The Results area of Cambridge support offers these resources.

questions.q: What is the best description of the 2024 to 2026 Listening paper?
questions.why: Paper 2 is 100 per cent multiple choice with 40 marks.

questions.q: What happened to tiers in the 2024 to 2026 syllabus?
o: Tiers were only used for Speaking
questions.why: The changes section says tiering has been removed from the qualification.

questions.q: Which phrase from the syllabus is a way of giving an example when speaking?
questions.why: The syllabus lists 'just to name a few' for exemplifying.

questions.q: Which pair are linking words that show contrast?
questions.why: However and whereas show contrast. Therefore and consequently show result.

questions.q: A student reads slowly because they try to understand every word. Which strategy helps most?
o: Give them a dictionary in the exam
Teach skimming, scanning and guessing meaning from context
Tell them to avoid long texts
Ask them to read the text three times
questions.why: Dictionaries are not allowed and strategies save time in 400 to 650 word texts.

questions.q: In Paper 2 Exercise 4 there are six speakers and eight statements. What does this mean for students?
o: Every statement must be used once
Two statements are not used, so students can cross out used ones
questions.why: Six speakers match six statements, so two statements are not used.

questions.q: Which is the best use of the one-minute preparation in Speaking Part 2?
o: Choose three ideas and an example in your head, without notes
Read the card aloud to the examiner
questions.why: Candidates are not allowed to write notes during preparation.

questions.q: In writing marking, what do you do after choosing the best-fit level?
o: Choose the mark inside the level: top, middle or lowest
questions.why: Convincingly meets: highest mark. Adequately: middle. Just meets: lowest.

questions.q: Which is a common teacher marking error?
o: Giving marks for effort or length instead of the mark scheme
questions.why: Marks must follow the mark scheme only.

questions.q: A student's short answer has a small spelling error but the meaning is clear. What is the usual rule?
o: Give the mark, since spelling is not tested there
questions.why: Spelling and grammar are judged only where the question tests them, if meaning is unambiguous.

questions.q: In Exercise 3, 'renting an e-bike' written as a policy in Question 8 earns:
o: 0 marks, it is the writer's own action
questions.why: It belongs under what the writer has tried, Question 9.

questions.q: Which statement matches Level 5 Development in the Speaking marking criteria?
o: Responses are relevant and consistently well developed; communication is maintained with ease
Responses are mostly relevant but limited
questions.why: That is the Level 5 (9 to 10 marks) wording.

questions.q: What should you do if more than one teacher in your centre marks Speaking?
o: Ask students to mark each other
Carry out internal moderation so all candidates are marked to the same standard
Mark separately and send different marks
questions.why: Cambridge requires moderation or standardisation when more than one teacher marks.

questions.q: Which of these must be true of the Speaking test recording?
o: It must be recorded in full for every candidate
Only the best candidates need a recording
questions.why: The test must be recorded in full for all candidates.

questions.q: Which is NOT a Speaking marking criterion?
questions.why: The four criteria are grammar, vocabulary, development and pronunciation.

questions.q: Which feedback is most helpful to a student?
o: A long list of every error
Two or three specific targets linked to a skill and an action
questions.why: Specific, limited targets with actions help students improve.

questions.q: What is the aim of a standardisation meeting?
questions.why: Standardisation creates consistent marking.

questions.q: A student writes a very long email far above the word range. What is likely?
o: Accuracy and control may suffer, and length alone earns no extra marks

questions.q: What is a distractor in multiple choice?

questions.why: Distractors may use words from the text but give the wrong meaning.

questions.q: In the Cambridge guide, what is the 'experienced curriculum'?

questions.why: The experienced curriculum is what learners really experience, including planned and unplanned outcomes.

questions.q: Which describes a 'spiral approach' to learning?
o: Each stage returns to key ideas and builds on them
Teaching each topic once and never returning
questions.why: In a spiral, learners revisit key learning areas at each stage.

questions.q: Who writes the schemes of work and lesson plans that make a Cambridge syllabus locally relevant?
questions.why: Cambridge says schools must create their own schemes of work and lessons.

questions.q: How are Cambridge examiners asked to treat spelling and grammar in subjects that are not language tests?

questions.q: Which is the correct age guidance for Cambridge Lower Secondary?

questions.q: What is an AS Level?

questions.why: An AS Level contains half the content of the corresponding A Level.

questions.why: A is basic, B is independent, C is proficient.

questions.q: About how many guided learning hours are recommended for a Cambridge IGCSE subject?
questions.why: Cambridge suggests about 130 hours per IGCSE or O Level subject.

questions.q: Which is a problem of very short lesson periods, according to the guide?
o: Lessons can become dominated by whole-class teaching
questions.why: There is a tendency for shorter periods to be dominated by whole-class instruction.

questions.q: What does CLIL stand for?
questions.why: CLIL: content and language integrated learning.

questions.q: What did Vygotsky call the area just beyond what a learner can do alone but can do with help?
questions.why: Teachers scaffold learning within this zone.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the five Cambridge learner attributes?
questions.why: The five are confident, responsible, reflective, innovative and engaged.

questions.q: According to the guide, how should ICT be used in the classroom?
o: To support carefully planned teaching and learning goals, not replace them
questions.why: Technology must enhance planned goals, not replace them.

questions.q: How many weeks should be used for new lessons in a 36 to 40 week school year?
questions.why: Leave the last 6 to 8 weeks as an exam buffer.

questions.q: What is a thematic module?
o: A 4 to 6 week block built around one popular topic
questions.why: Modules group about 4 to 6 weeks around a theme such as travel or health.

questions.q: Which column is NOT in the medium-term scheme of work described in this course?
questions.why: The four columns are theme and timeline, language focus, exam skill focus and assessment goal.

questions.q: Which of these is a good learning target?
o: I can write a magazine article with a clear introduction and conclusion
questions.why: A learning target says what the student will be able to do.

questions.q: Which CEFR range should students ideally have when starting IGCSE ESL?
questions.why: Strong A2 to lower B1 is the suggested entry level.

questions.q: Which is an example of a sentence mechanics problem?
questions.why: Subject-verb agreement is part of sentence mechanics.

questions.q: Which best describes the initial assessment?
o: A short ungraded diagnostic used to spot weaknesses early
questions.why: It is a diagnostic tool, not graded for a report card.

questions.q: In the 30-minute template, how long is the writing part?
questions.why: Part 1 is 15 minutes, Part 2 writing is 15 minutes and Part 3 speaking is 5 minutes per student.

questions.q: After the diagnostic, what should you do first?
o: Look for patterns across the class and adjust the plan
Give the same lesson to everyone
questions.why: Results are for planning and support, not ranking.

questions.q: In a KWL chart, what does the W column stand for?
questions.why: K is what I know, W is what I want to know and L is what I learned.

questions.q: Which four items make up the daily-teaching version of the scheme of work in Week 4?
o: Timeline and objectives, core tasks and skills, resources and technology, assessment methods
Theme, textbook, homework and mock exam
questions.why: The four columns are Timeline and objectives, Core tasks and skills, Resources and technology, and Assessment methods.

questions.q: A teacher writes the objective 'To do Exercise 3'. What is the main weakness?
o: It says what the page is, not what students will be able to do
questions.why: A good objective says what students can do, using a verb you can see or hear.

questions.q: What does the 'golden thread' link?
o: The starter, the plenary and the homework
Syllabus aim, module target, lesson objective, task and check
The three papers and their marks
The teacher, the head and the parents
questions.why: Each lesson should connect back to a syllabus aim and forward to a check.

questions.q: A scheme row says 'projector, audio file, speaker'. Which column is it in and what should be added?
o: Core tasks and skills, with a timer
Resources and technology, with a low-tech backup
Assessment methods, with a mark scheme
questions.why: Technology can fail, so every digital resource needs a low-tech backup.

questions.q: In a 55 minute lesson, which plan is most balanced?
o: Starter 6, input 10, guided practice 12, free production 15, plenary 8, close 2
questions.why: A balanced lesson has a short starter, three main phases and a plenary.

questions.q: A lesson is running late. What should the teacher do?
o: Speak faster and add more tasks
Shorten earlier phases or cut a task but keep the plenary
Keep going until the end of the book unit
Skip the plenary and give all remaining tasks as homework
questions.why: The plenary shows what students learned, so it should not be cut.

questions.q: What is the purpose of guided practice?
o: Students speak freely without any help
Students use new language with support in controlled tasks
The teacher reads the text aloud
questions.why: Guided practice gives support before free production.

questions.q: Which instruction check is best after explaining a pair task?
questions.why: A specific question shows whether students know what to do.

questions.q: Which activity is best as a starter?
o: Students copy the objective from the board
The teacher explains a new grammar rule for ten minutes
Students put a jumbled sentence in order in pairs
Students silently read a long text
questions.why: A good starter is short, active, uses English and needs little preparation.

questions.q: After exit tickets, what should a teacher do?
o: Sort them into got it, nearly and not yet, and plan the next lesson
Give them back the next term
questions.why: Checks are useful only when the teacher acts on them.

questions.q: Which pattern of vocabulary review works best?
o: Review after one day, one week and one month
Teach twenty words once and test at the end of the year
Review only words students ask about
questions.why: Spaced review helps words move into long-term memory.

questions.q: What is the correct order in the skills chain?
questions.why: Students first take in language, notice it, practise it and then produce it.

questions.q: A teacher uses the living stone plants article for reading, then a pair task giving advice, then an email. What pattern is this?
o: Reading, speaking and writing around one language pattern
questions.why: One text supports several skills when you choose a pattern to notice.

questions.q: Why is the final output task important in an integrated sequence?
o: It is the only exam skill
Students need to use the language, not only recognise it
questions.why: Without output, students recognise but cannot use the language.

questions.q: When should full timed past papers mainly be used?
o: Every week from the first day
At the end of modules, in mocks and in the final term
questions.why: Use earlier stages to learn tasks and skills before timing full papers.

questions.q: After students do a past paper, what is the most useful next step?
o: Put the scripts in a file
Mark with the mark scheme, find errors and redo
Move on to a new topic
questions.why: Review and redo turns practice into learning.

questions.q: How many marks and questions does the 2024 specimen Paper 1 have?
questions.why: The specimen paper has 17 questions and 60 marks.

questions.q: In the specimen mark scheme, what does Question 6 ask for?
o: Any three of four advice details about growing living stone plants
questions.why: Question 6 is worth three marks for three advice details.

questions.q: In specimen Exercise 3, how many marks are given for disadvantages and for reasons for popularity?
questions.why: Question 8 gives three marks and Question 9 gives four marks.

questions.q: In specimen Question 17, students write a report and must also do what?
o: Use some of the comment ideas and some ideas of their own
questions.why: Content marks depend on developing ideas, not copying.

questions.q: Why did students lose a mark for 'charging drivers' in a notes answer?
o: It was in the wrong order
It was incomplete; it needed 'to enter parts of the city'
questions.why: Notes must carry the key meaning from the text.

questions.q: In Exercise 2, the key word 'suggests' tells the student to look for what?
o: Implied meaning, not only a fact
questions.why: The examiner report says implied meaning was hard for many students.

questions.q: A student writes 'I really wanted to take place in the event.' What is the error?
questions.why: The examiner report lists this common confusion.

questions.q: For Paper 3, the examiner report says many centres marked pronunciation in what way?
o: Not as a stand-alone criterion, matching it to other marks
questions.why: Pronunciation must be marked on its own evidence.

questions.q: Which activity is an information gap?
o: Students fill gaps with one verb
Student A has the morning timetable and Student B the afternoon; they ask each other to complete it
questions.why: Each student has information the other needs.

questions.q: When is delayed correction best?
o: During a fluency discussion, with errors reviewed afterwards
questions.why: Interrupting a fluency task can stop communication.

questions.q: What is the best way to increase Student Talking Time in a class of 40?
o: One student speaks at a time
questions.why: Pair work gives many students speaking time at once.

questions.q: A teacher says 'CLT means no grammar'. What is the best reply?
o: Grammar is taught, but through use in communicative tasks
questions.why: CLT teaches grammar in context.

questions.q: What are the three stages of the Willis framework?
o: Pre-task, task cycle and language focus
questions.why: Willis's 1996 framework has these three stages.

questions.q: In TBL, when does the main focus on language form take place?
o: After the task, in the language focus
questions.why: Students use language first and then study it.

questions.q: What are the three parts of the task cycle?
questions.why: Students do the task, plan their report and report to the class.

questions.q: Which is the best reason to use PPP for conditionals and TBL for fluency?
o: PPP gives a clear structure for specific grammar, and TBL builds fluency
questions.why: A good teacher uses both for different purposes.

questions.q: What is the correct timing for Paper 3 Part 2?
o: 3 to 4 minutes including 1 minute of preparation
questions.why: Students prepare for one minute and talk for up to two minutes.

questions.q: What pattern do the three Part 1 questions follow?
o: Present or habits, a past story, an opinion or future
questions.why: The teacher's notes show this pattern.

questions.q: What do weaker Part 2 talks often do, according to the examiner report?
o: Talk about only one option or not state a preference
questions.why: Students should cover both options and state a preference.

questions.q: What should the examiner do if a candidate does not start speaking after 15 seconds in Part 2?
o: Read the prompt: Are you ready to start talking about the points on the card?
questions.why: The notes give exact prompts.

questions.q: What should the answer key for Exercise 1 style short answers show?
o: The correct answer and acceptable alternatives, with brackets for words not needed
questions.why: This matches the style of the Cambridge mark scheme.

questions.q: Which statement about a multiple-choice distractor is true?
o: It should be 'all of the above'
It should never appear in the text
It should be mentioned in the text but not answer the question
questions.why: Good distractors are tempting because they use text words.

questions.q: Which task is a good Part 2 card?
o: A long text to read aloud
One option and a yes or no question
Two realistic options and a request to compare and say which you prefer and why
questions.why: It copies the Cambridge pattern.

questions.q: Which statement about endorsed textbooks is correct?
o: They are written by Cambridge examiners for each class
They match the syllabus but do not replace it or fit every class
questions.why: Endorsement is a check of fit, not a replacement.

questions.q: What is scaffolding?
o: Temporary support that is removed as students improve
questions.why: Scaffolds help students until they can work alone.

questions.q: Which checklist item is student-friendly?
o: I answered all three bullet points
questions.why: Use simple 'I' statements.

questions.q: What must follow a self-assessment checklist?
o: One change or target to improve the work
questions.why: Checking is useful only when it leads to action.

questions.q: Which is a good first step when teaching students to use a checklist?
o: Give it out with no instructions
Model it on a sample answer, thinking aloud
questions.why: Students need to see how it works first.

questions.q: Which action best fits a 90-day plan for a teacher?
o: Teach three lessons from the new plan, start a tracker and review with a colleague
Change the whole course at once
questions.why: Small steps, tracked and shared, make lasting change.
